root.stem: A 7-month-old girl whose parents come from Cyprus is brought in because she has become pale and irritable over 4 weeks and feeds poorly. She was well at birth. Both parents have had mild anemia that did not improve with iron tablets. She has mild jaundice, and her liver and spleen are enlarged. Hemoglobin is 5.8 g/dL and mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is 58 fL. The blood smear shows small pale red cells, target cells and nucleated red cells, with no spherocytes and no sickle cells. Serum ferritin is high. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows mostly fetal hemoglobin (HbF) with no hemoglobin A (HbA), no hemoglobin S, and no hemoglobin H or Bart; both parents' electrophoresis shows a raised hemoglobin A2 (HbA2). Osmotic fragility is normal.
root.oneliner: 7mo F + Cypriot parents + pale and irritable over 4 weeks, well at birth + parents with mild anemia unresponsive to iron + mild jaundice + enlarged liver and spleen + Hb 5.8, MCV 58 + small pale cells, target cells, nucleated red cells, no spherocytes or sickle cells + high ferritin + mostly HbF, no HbA, HbS, H or Bart + parents' HbA2 raised + normal osmotic fragility
highlight: did not improve with iron tablets
small pale red cells, target cells and nucleated red cells
no spherocytes and no sickle cells
mostly fetal hemoglobin (HbF) with no hemoglobin A (HbA)

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An inherited failure to make enough beta-globin chains. The clincher: **severe microcytic anemia from about 4-6 months of age + target cells and nucleated red cells + mostly fetal hemoglobin with no hemoglobin A + enlarged liver and spleen**, with normal iron stores.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Cooley anemia and thalassemia major are the same disease.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Two beta-null alleles give no hemoglobin A and mostly fetal hemoglobin; carriers show a raised hemoglobin A2.

nodes.q: Her electrophoresis shows mostly fetal hemoglobin. Why was she well at birth and ill by 7 months?
nodes.a: Fetal hemoglobin (two alpha and two gamma chains) needs no beta chains, and it falls after birth
nodes.note: Beta chains should replace gamma chains in the first months of life; without them, no adult hemoglobin A is made and the anemia appears at about 4-6 months.

nodes.q: How is it inherited?
nodes.note: Both parents carry one faulty beta-globin gene (chromosome 11); each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 risk of an affected child.

nodes.q: What do her parents have?
nodes.a: Beta-thalassemia minor (trait): mild microcytic anemia with a raised hemoglobin A2
nodes.note: Carriers usually have no symptoms or only mild anemia; it does not respond to iron, and ferritin is normal.

nodes.q: Suppose instead one parent carried a null allele (no beta-globin) and the other carried a milder allele that halves the output of that gene. What would a child who inherits both faulty alleles have?
nodes.a: Thalassemia intermedia (about 25% of normal beta-globin function, needing occasional transfusions)
nodes.note: One in four children inherit both faulty alleles. A child with two null alleles has thalassemia major with no hemoglobin A; a milder allele leaves some hemoglobin A and a milder course.

nodes.q: What kind of mutation usually causes it?
nodes.a: Point mutations that disturb how the beta-globin messenger RNA is made (not large gene deletions)
nodes.note: Deletions are the usual cause of alpha-thalassemia; in beta-thalassemia, hundreds of point mutations reduce (beta-plus) or abolish (beta-zero) beta-chain production.

nodes.q: Her short supply of beta chains comes from an error in processing the first messenger RNA transcript. A single base change at which part of the gene does this?
nodes.a: A splice site (the GT donor or AG acceptor at an intron-exon border)
nodes.note: Introns must be cut out of the first transcript. A change at a conserved splice site leaves the transcript wrongly spliced, so little or no normal beta-globin is made. Changes in the start codon or stop codon affect translation, and promoter changes affect transcription, not processing. In Cyprus and the eastern Mediterranean the most common allele is a splice mutation in the first intron.

nodes.q: Which cellular machinery recognises the splice sites and is blocked when they mutate?
nodes.note: They bind the donor and acceptor sites to cut out the intron; transport, capping and signal recognition particles are not involved.

nodes.q: A different point mutation deep inside an intron creates a new AG sequence. What does the splicing machinery do with it?
nodes.a: Uses it as a new 3' splice site, so part of the intron stays in the messenger RNA and little normal beta-globin is made
nodes.note: The abnormal messenger RNA is degraded or encodes a useless chain; this is a beta-plus type mutation.

nodes.q: A point mutation changes the signal AATAAA to AACAAA beyond the coding region. Which step of messenger RNA processing is lost?
nodes.a: Cleavage and polyadenylation of the 3' end
nodes.note: Without the poly-A tail the messenger RNA is unstable, so the beta-globin messenger RNA falls to about 10% of normal. Capping, splicing and transport are unaffected.

nodes.q: What goes wrong inside her red cell precursors?
nodes.a: An imbalance of globin chains: excess alpha chains precipitate and destroy the cells
nodes.note: Alpha chains normally pair with beta chains; unpaired alpha chains form inclusions, so red cells die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) and in the spleen. In alpha-thalassemia it is the excess beta chains that form tetramers instead.

nodes.q: Which skull X-ray appearance develops in untreated children because the marrow expands?
nodes.note: Expanded marrow also causes frontal bossing and an overgrown upper jaw ('chipmunk face'); extramedullary hematopoiesis enlarges the liver and spleen.

nodes.q: Her marrow already works at full stretch. Which virus can suddenly stop red cell production and drop her hemoglobin to dangerous levels?
nodes.note: The virus infects red cell precursors through the P antigen; the reticulocyte count falls to near zero. Any chronic hemolytic anemia is at risk.

nodes.q: Regular transfusions plus extra iron absorbed from the gut cause which complication?
nodes.note: Ineffective erythropoiesis lowers hepcidin, so the gut absorbs more iron on top of the transfused iron.

nodes.q: Which organ failure is the usual cause of death?
nodes.a: **Heart failure and arrhythmias from iron-overload cardiomyopathy**
nodes.note: Iron also damages the liver, pancreas and pituitary and gonads (diabetes, delayed puberty).

nodes.q: What is the standard treatment?
nodes.a: Regular red cell transfusions every few weeks
nodes.note: Keeps hemoglobin above about 9-10 g/dL and suppresses the expanded marrow.

nodes.q: Which drugs prevent iron overload from the transfusions?
nodes.a: Iron chelators such as deferoxamine or oral deferasirox
nodes.note: Deferoxamine is given by subcutaneous or intravenous infusion; deferasirox and deferiprone are oral (deferiprone can cause agranulocytosis).

nodes.q: Which treatment can cure the disease?
nodes.note: Best results are in young children with a matched sibling donor before iron damage builds up.

nodes.q: Her microcytic anemia with target cells could suggest alpha-thalassemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Alpha-gene deletions; **hemoglobin Bart in newborns and hemoglobin H later, with normal hemoglobin A2 and fetal hemoglobin**; more common in Southeast Asia and Africa
Beta-gene point mutations; **no hemoglobin A, high fetal hemoglobin, ill after the first months** and raised hemoglobin A2 in carriers; Mediterranean ancestry

nodes.note: The trap: both are inherited, microcytic and unresponsive to iron, with target cells.

nodes.q: Her small pale red cells could suggest iron deficiency anemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low ferritin, high total iron-binding capacity** and improvement with iron; no target cells or nucleated red cells
**High ferritin, no response to iron + target cells + fetal hemoglobin**

nodes.q: Her anemia with jaundice and an enlarged spleen could suggest sickle cell disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hemoglobin S on electrophoresis + sickle cells**, painful crises and dactylitis; the cells are not small
**No hemoglobin S; small cells with target cells and nucleated red cells**, no pain crises

nodes.q: Her jaundice and enlarged spleen could suggest hereditary spherocytosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Spherocytes without central pallor + raised mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration + abnormal osmotic fragility**; normal mean corpuscular volume
**Small cells and target cells, osmotic fragility normal or decreased, no spherocytes**

root.stem: A newborn boy becomes deeply yellow 10 hours after birth. His mother is 28 years old, blood group O Rh-negative, and her only earlier pregnancy ended in a miscarriage at 12 weeks; she received no injection afterward. The father is Rh-positive. The baby is blood group O Rh-positive, pale, with an enlarged liver and spleen. Hemoglobin is low, the reticulocyte count is high, indirect bilirubin is raised and the direct Coombs test is strongly positive. Platelet count is normal, and the mother and father are of Irish descent.
root.oneliner: Newborn M + jaundice at 10 hours + mother O Rh-negative with earlier miscarriage at 12 weeks and no anti-D injection + Rh-positive father + baby O Rh-positive, pale, enlarged liver and spleen + low hemoglobin, high reticulocytes, high indirect bilirubin + strongly positive direct Coombs + normal platelets + Irish parents
highlight: direct Coombs test is strongly positive

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Hemolytic disease of the newborn from Rh(D) incompatibility
nodes.note: Maternal antibodies against the baby's red cell D antigen destroy the baby's red cells. The clincher: **jaundice in the first 24 hours + Rh-negative mother with an Rh-positive baby + positive direct Coombs test + anemia with high reticulocytes**. Jaundice in the first 24 hours is never physiologic.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The name refers to the nucleated red cell precursors (erythroblasts) released into the fetal blood.

nodes.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction destroys the baby's red cells?
nodes.note: Anti-D IgG coats the fetal red cells, which macrophages in the spleen remove (extravascular hemolysis). The same mechanism, antibody against a cell-surface target, is seen in Graves disease; peanut allergy is type I, and poison ivy and the tuberculin reaction are type IV.

nodes.q: Why did this Rh-positive pregnancy become dangerous only after her earlier miscarriage?
nodes.a: The miscarriage let Rh-positive fetal red cells enter her blood and sensitized her to the D antigen
nodes.note: Fetal blood enters the maternal circulation at delivery, miscarriage, abortion, ectopic pregnancy, bleeding, trauma or amniocentesis. The first response is small and slow, so the first Rh-positive baby is usually spared; memory B cells then respond fast in the next Rh-positive pregnancy.

nodes.q: Which antibody class made in that faster second response crosses the placenta to reach his red cells?
nodes.note: IgG is carried across the placenta by the neonatal Fc receptor on the trophoblast. IgM, made first, is too large to cross; this is also why the natural IgM anti-A and anti-B of most mothers do not harm the baby.

nodes.q: Which test shows antibody on the baby's red cells?
nodes.note: Positive in this baby; it detects IgG already bound to his red cells. It is negative in physiologic jaundice.

nodes.q: Severe anemia before birth can cause which fetal condition?
nodes.note: High-output heart failure and low albumin (the liver is busy making red cells instead of protein) give fluid in the skin, abdomen, chest and around the heart. **Untreated, it ends in stillbirth.** The liver and spleen enlarge from extramedullary hematopoiesis and release erythroblasts into the blood.

nodes.q: The destroyed red cells release heme. Which pigment rises and causes his jaundice?
nodes.note: Before birth the placenta clears it into the mother, so jaundice appears only after delivery; the newborn liver cannot conjugate the large load.

nodes.q: Which brain injury can the high level cause?
nodes.note: Lipid-soluble bilirubin enters the basal ganglia, causing athetoid cerebral palsy, hearing loss and gaze palsy.

nodes.q: Which treatment is started first to lower his bilirubin?
nodes.note: Blue-green light turns bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble isomers (lumirubin) that are excreted without conjugation. Intravenous immune globulin can reduce hemolysis in Rh disease.

nodes.q: His bilirubin keeps rising toward the toxic range despite phototherapy. Which procedure removes both the bilirubin and the antibody-coated red cells?
nodes.note: Uses group O Rh-negative blood. Before birth, severe fetal anemia is treated by intrauterine transfusion through the umbilical vein.

nodes.q: At the first prenatal visit, which test on an Rh-negative woman shows whether she already has anti-D in her serum?
nodes.note: If anti-D is already present she is sensitized: anti-D immune globulin no longer helps, and the titer and the fetal middle cerebral artery Doppler are followed instead.

nodes.q: Her anti-D titer is rising in a later pregnancy. Which ultrasound measurement detects fetal anemia without a needle?
nodes.a: Peak systolic velocity in the fetal middle cerebral artery
nodes.note: Anemia lowers blood viscosity and raises cardiac output, so velocity rises; amniocentesis for bilirubin is no longer the first test.

nodes.q: Which drug given to an unsensitized Rh-negative mother prevents the disease?
nodes.a: Anti-D immune globulin (Rho(D) immune globulin, RhoGAM)
nodes.note: Pooled human IgG against the D antigen. It works only if she has not yet made her own anti-D.

nodes.q: When is it routinely given in pregnancy and after birth?
nodes.a: At about 28 weeks' gestation, and again within 72 hours of delivery if the baby is Rh-positive
nodes.note: Also within 72 hours of miscarriage, abortion, ectopic pregnancy, amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling, vaginal bleeding, abdominal trauma or external cephalic version. The 28-week dose covers silent bleeds in the third trimester; giving it at 28 weeks does not harm the fetus.

nodes.q: After delivery, which test measures how much fetal blood entered her circulation so the dose can be increased if needed?
nodes.note: A rosette test screens first; fetal hemoglobin resists acid, so fetal cells stay pink. Flow cytometry can be used instead. One standard 300 µg dose covers about 30 mL of fetal whole blood.

nodes.q: What kind of immunization is it?
nodes.a: Passive immunization: the given antibody binds and clears the Rh(D) antigen on fetal cells before her immune system responds
nodes.note: It is not a vaccine (not active immunization) and does not make her produce antibodies; corticosteroids have no role.

nodes.q: Given at 28 weeks to an Rh-negative woman carrying the baby of an Rh-positive man, which process does it prevent in the mother?
nodes.a: Sensitization (alloimmunization): her own production of anti-D antibodies and memory B cells
nodes.note: Without memory B cells, later Rh-positive babies are spared. The drug protects future pregnancies; it does not treat a fetus already affected.

nodes.q: His early jaundice with a positive Coombs test could suggest ABO incompatibility. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Mother group O with a **group A or B baby**; group O mothers naturally make some IgG anti-A and anti-B, so the **first pregnancy can be affected**; spherocytes, weakly positive Coombs test, usually mild and rarely causes hydrops. The most common cause of hemolytic disease of the newborn overall.
**Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive baby, prior sensitizing event**; strongly positive Coombs test, severe anemia, can cause hydrops. His **blood group is O**, so ABO disease is impossible.

nodes.note: The trap: both give jaundice in the first day with a positive Coombs test. Fetal red cells carry few A and B antigens, which is why ABO disease is mild.

nodes.q: His severe hemolysis before birth could have caused hydrops, which can also come from alpha-thalassemia major. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Four alpha genes deleted; Southeast Asian parents; **hemoglobin Bart and a negative Coombs test**
**Rh-negative mother with anti-D and a positive Coombs test**; normal hemoglobin electrophoresis

nodes.q: A maternal antibody against a fetal blood cell antigen could also mean fetal alloimmune thrombocytopenia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Maternal IgG against a fetal platelet antigen (usually HPA-1a); **low platelets with petechiae or brain bleeding, normal hemoglobin and bilirubin**; can affect the first pregnancy
**Anemia with jaundice and a positive Coombs test**; platelets normal

nodes.q: Other causes of newborn jaundice or fetal anemia were possible. Which finding rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Appears after 24 hours, peaks on days 3 to 5**, normal hemoglobin, negative Coombs test
Onset at 10 hours, anemia and a positive Coombs test
**Fetal anemia with a very low reticulocyte count and a negative Coombs test** (nonimmune hydrops)
High reticulocytes and a positive Coombs test
Family history, **spherocytes with a negative Coombs test**
Positive Coombs test and an Rh-negative mother

root.stem: A 61-year-old woman has had 8 months of tiredness, breathlessness on climbing stairs and a sore, smooth red tongue. For 3 months she has had burning in her feet and numbness that has spread to her calves, and she has begun to stumble in the dark. She eats meat and dairy and drinks little alcohol, takes no zinc or antifolate drugs, and has had no stomach surgery. Vibration and position sense are lost at the ankles. Hemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is 118 fL and the reticulocyte count is low. The smear shows oval macrocytes and neutrophils with six lobes. Marrow biopsy shows a hypercellular marrow with large precursor cells. Serum vitamin B12 is low, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are raised, folate, copper and thyroid-stimulating hormone are normal, and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are present.
root.oneliner: 61F + 8 months fatigue, exertional dyspnea, sore smooth red tongue + burning feet, numbness to calves, stumbling in the dark + eats meat, no zinc or antifolate drugs, no gastric surgery + lost vibration and position sense + Hb 8.4, MCV 118, low reticulocytes + oval macrocytes, six-lobed neutrophils + hypercellular marrow with megaloblasts + low B12, high methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, normal folate, copper and TSH + anti-intrinsic factor antibodies
highlight: takes no zinc or antifolate drugs
Vibration and position sense are lost
oval macrocytes and neutrophils with six lobes
hypercellular marrow with large precursor cells
methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are raised
folate, copper and thyroid-stimulating hormone are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Vitamin B12 deficiency from autoimmune destruction of the stomach's intrinsic factor supply. The clincher: **macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils + sore tongue + loss of vibration and position sense + anti-intrinsic factor and antiparietal cell antibodies**.

nodes.q: Which stomach cells are destroyed?
nodes.note: They lie in the body and fundus of the stomach and make hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, the protein that carries vitamin B12 to the terminal ileum for absorption.

nodes.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction produces the antibodies against these cells?
nodes.note: Antibodies to the parietal cell proton pump and to intrinsic factor, with T-cell damage, lead to atrophic gastritis of the body and fundus.

nodes.q: Her marrow shows large precursor cells whose nuclei look immature while the cytoplasm looks mature. What is this change called?
nodes.note: DNA synthesis lags behind RNA and protein synthesis. In the blood it shows as macro-ovalocytes and neutrophils with five or more lobes; many precursors die in the marrow, so reticulocytes are low.

nodes.q: Which vitamin B12-dependent reaction explains the megaloblastic cells?
nodes.a: Homocysteine to methionine by methionine synthase, which regenerates tetrahydrofolate
nodes.note: Without it, folate is trapped as methyl-tetrahydrofolate, so thymidylate and DNA synthesis fail while RNA and protein keep growing the cell.

nodes.q: Which vitamin B12-dependent reaction is blamed for the nerve damage?
nodes.a: Methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
nodes.note: Methylmalonic acid builds up and abnormal fatty acids enter myelin.

nodes.q: Which spinal cord tracts are damaged?
nodes.a: **Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts (subacute combined degeneration)**
nodes.note: Causes loss of vibration and position sense, ataxia and spasticity. It can become irreversible if untreated.

nodes.q: Which blood level is raised in vitamin B12 deficiency but not in folate deficiency?
nodes.note: Homocysteine rises in both, because both vitamins are needed for methionine synthase.

nodes.q: Which antibody test is the most specific?
nodes.note: Antiparietal cell antibodies are more sensitive but less specific. Gastrin is high and pepsinogen I is low.

nodes.q: Which autoimmune thyroid disease is most often found alongside it?
nodes.note: Pernicious anemia clusters with other organ-specific autoimmune diseases: type 1 diabetes, vitiligo and Addison disease.

nodes.q: Which cancer risk is raised by the atrophic gastritis?
nodes.note: Surveillance endoscopy is considered; the high gastrin also promotes carcinoid tumors.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.note: Oral high-dose can work, but injections are standard. Giving folate alone fixes the blood count but lets the nerve damage worsen.

nodes.q: Within a week of treatment, which blood count rises first?
nodes.note: Monitor potassium: new red cell production can lower it.

nodes.q: Her macrocytic anemia could suggest folate deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Poor diet, alcohol or antifolate drugs; **normal methylmalonic acid, no neurologic findings**, high homocysteine; no antibodies
**High methylmalonic acid + loss of vibration and position sense + anti-intrinsic factor antibodies**

nodes.note: The trap: both give megaloblastic anemia and high homocysteine.

nodes.q: Her numb feet and unsteady gait could suggest copper deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: After bariatric surgery or excess zinc; **low copper and ceruloplasmin, often with neutropenia**, mimics the spinal cord picture; vitamin B12 normal
**Low vitamin B12 with high methylmalonic acid + intrinsic factor antibodies**; no zinc excess or surgery

nodes.q: Her fatigue with a high mean corpuscular volume could suggest hypothyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Mild macrocytosis, cold intolerance, weight gain; **high thyroid-stimulating hormone**, normal nerve examination, no megaloblasts
**Megaloblasts with hypersegmented neutrophils + dorsal column loss**; normal thyroid-stimulating hormone

nodes.q: Her low blood counts could suggest aplastic anemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pancytopenia with an empty, hypocellular marrow**; normal-sized red cells
**Hypercellular marrow with megaloblasts + macrocytes**

root.stem: A 29-year-old woman has had 3 months of tiredness and dark red-brown urine that is worst on waking and clears during the day. She has had two episodes of crampy upper abdominal pain, and her abdomen has become swollen. She has no family history of anemia, has not eaten fava beans, and takes no medications. She has scleral icterus, a tender enlarged liver and ascites. Hemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL with a normal mean corpuscular volume, lactate dehydrogenase is raised, haptoglobin is low and the platelet count is mildly low. The smear shows no spherocytes or bite cells. The direct Coombs test is negative, and the acidified serum test is positive. Flow cytometry shows that many of her red and white cells lack two surface proteins that protect cells from complement.
root.oneliner: 29F + 3 months fatigue + dark urine worst on waking + abdominal pain, swelling + no family history, no fava beans, no drugs + icterus, tender enlarged liver, ascites + Hb 8.6, normal MCV, high LDH, low haptoglobin, mild thrombocytopenia + no spherocytes or bite cells + Coombs negative + acidified serum test positive + flow cytometry: red and white cells lack two complement-protecting proteins
highlight: dark red-brown urine that is worst on waking
lack two surface proteins that protect cells from complement

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An acquired stem cell disease in which complement destroys the red cells. The clincher: **Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis + dark morning urine + venous thrombosis in an unusual site, with blood cells missing their complement-protecting proteins**.

nodes.q: Which cell-surface defect makes the red cells vulnerable?
nodes.a: Failure to make the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor that attaches membrane proteins
nodes.note: An acquired PIGA gene mutation in a blood stem cell; all red cells, white cells and platelets from that clone are affected, so the defect is not inherited.

nodes.q: Which proteins that normally shield the cell from complement are missing?
nodes.a: CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis)
nodes.note: Without them, the membrane attack complex assembles on the cell and punches holes in it.

nodes.q: Why is the urine darkest in the morning?
nodes.a: Slight acidosis during sleep promotes complement activation, and the urine is concentrated overnight
nodes.note: Carbon dioxide rises with shallow breathing in sleep, but hemolysis occurs around the clock.

nodes.q: Which kind of hemolysis is this?
nodes.note: Free hemoglobin lowers haptoglobin, raises lactate dehydrogenase and spills into urine (hemoglobinuria, then hemosiderinuria).

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis today?
nodes.a: Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 on red and white cells
nodes.note: The older acidified serum (Ham) test, positive in her, and the sucrose lysis test were used before; FLAER, a reagent that binds the anchor itself, is added to flow cytometry. The Coombs test is negative.

nodes.q: Which complication is the leading cause of death?
nodes.note: Free hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide and platelets are activated; hepatic, portal, cerebral and mesenteric veins clot.

nodes.q: Hepatic vein thrombosis causes which syndrome?
nodes.note: Abdominal pain, tender liver enlargement and ascites.

nodes.q: Which bone marrow disease is closely linked?
nodes.note: The clone expands in a failing marrow; some patients later develop myelodysplasia or acute myeloid leukemia.

nodes.q: Which deficiency develops over time from the urine losses?
nodes.note: Hemosiderin is lost in the urine; iron replacement can trigger hemolysis.

nodes.q: Which drug class stops the hemolysis?
nodes.note: Monoclonal antibodies block formation of the membrane attack complex.

nodes.q: Which infection risk requires vaccination before starting?
nodes.note: The membrane attack complex (C5b-9) is needed to kill encapsulated Neisseria, so meningococcal vaccines are given at least 2 weeks before the first dose.

nodes.q: Which treatment can cure the disease?
nodes.note: Reserved for severe marrow failure or life-threatening thrombosis.

nodes.q: Her dark urine could suggest G6PD deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: X-linked, usually a man; **episodes after fava beans, sulfa drugs or infection + bite cells and Heinz bodies**
**Dark morning urine with no trigger + thrombosis + absent CD55 and CD59**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis.

nodes.q: Her anemia with jaundice could suggest autoimmune hemolytic anemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Positive direct Coombs test + spherocytes**; mainly extravascular
**Negative Coombs test + hemoglobinuria + absent CD55 and CD59**

nodes.q: Her jaundice could suggest hereditary spherocytosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Family history; **spherocytes + raised mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration + abnormal osmotic fragility**; extravascular
**No spherocytes, no family history, hemoglobinuria with complement-mediated hemolysis**

nodes.q: Her anemia could suggest thalassemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Inherited, **small red cells with target cells, abnormal hemoglobin electrophoresis**, onset in childhood
**Normal-sized red cells, normal electrophoresis, adult onset with hemoglobinuria**

root.stem: A 23-year-old woman develops fever of 39.5°C, chills and foul-smelling vaginal discharge 2 days after an elective termination of pregnancy. On the next morning she is short of breath and has passed very little urine. She has petechiae on her legs, bruises on her arms and oozing from her intravenous site. She is alert, with no confusion or focal weakness, and blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg. Platelet count is 38,000/mm3, prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times are prolonged, and D-dimer is markedly raised. The smear shows fragmented red cells, and creatinine is rising.
root.oneliner: 23F + fever 39.5°C, chills, foul discharge 2 days after elective termination + next day dyspnea, oliguria + petechiae, bruises, oozing IV site + alert, no confusion + BP 82/50 + platelets 38,000 + prolonged PT and PTT + very high D-dimer + schistocytes + rising creatinine
highlight: prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times are prolonged

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Widespread clotting that uses up platelets and clotting factors, so the patient clots and bleeds at once. The clincher: **a trigger such as sepsis + bleeding from several sites + low platelets, prolonged prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times and a high D-dimer**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same process.

nodes.q: Which trigger set it off in her?
nodes.a: Sepsis (bacterial endotoxin) from an infected uterus after the termination
nodes.note: Other classic triggers: placental abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, a retained dead fetus, trauma, snake bites and cancer.

nodes.q: Which leukemia is the classic malignant cause?
nodes.note: Release of granule contents activates clotting.

nodes.q: Which molecule starts the widespread clotting?
nodes.a: Tissue factor, which triggers the extrinsic pathway and a burst of thrombin
nodes.note: Endotoxin and cytokines make endothelial cells and monocytes express it; thrombin forms microthrombi everywhere.

nodes.q: Which clotting protein, measured in plasma, is classically low in her because it is used up to build the clots?
nodes.note: Fibrinogen is consumed as fibrin forms; platelets and factors V and VIII also fall. Bleeding time is prolonged, not decreased.

nodes.q: Her D-dimer is markedly raised. Which enzyme produces it by breaking down the microthrombi?
nodes.note: Plasmin cleaves cross-linked fibrin into D-dimers and other fibrin degradation products, which themselves inhibit clotting and add to the bleeding.

nodes.q: What cuts her red cells into fragments?
nodes.a: Fibrin strands in the small vessels (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia)
nodes.note: The fragments are called schistocytes; they are also seen in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and hemolytic uremic syndrome.

nodes.q: Which organs failed to cause her breathlessness and low urine output?
nodes.note: The result is acute respiratory distress syndrome and acute kidney injury, with multiorgan failure.

nodes.q: What kills most patients?
nodes.a: **Multiorgan failure and hemorrhage, including intracranial bleeding**
nodes.note: Mortality is high despite treatment.

nodes.q: What is the first priority in management?
nodes.a: Treat the underlying cause (antibiotics and removal of infected uterine tissue)

root.stem: A 62-year-old man is seen before knee surgery and feels well. He has no fever, night sweats, weight loss or recent infection, and no lymph nodes or spleen can be felt. Leukocyte count is 11,500/mm3 with 52% small mature lymphocytes, hemoglobin is 14.2 g/dL and platelet count is 245,000/mm3. Flow cytometry shows 2,800 B cells per µL; they are CD5-positive, CD23-positive, CD10-negative and cyclin D1-negative, with surface kappa on 94% and lambda on 3%. T-cell subsets are normal.

highlight: no fever, night sweats, weight loss or recent infection
no lymph nodes or spleen can be felt
surface kappa on 94% and lambda on 3%

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A small clone of identical B cells in a well person. The clincher: **fewer than 5,000 clonal B cells per µL + one light-chain type on flow cytometry + no lymph nodes, large spleen, anemia or symptoms**.

nodes.q: Which flow cytometry result proves the B cells are one clone?
nodes.a: A skewed surface kappa-to-lambda light chain ratio (light-chain restriction)
nodes.note: Each B cell carries one light chain type; a normal polyclonal population has both, so a ratio above about 3:1 or below about 0.3:1 signals a clone. Absolute counts of lymphocytes, T cells or B cells and the CD4:CD8 ratio can all be raised by reactive causes.

nodes.q: Which marker, usually found on T cells, is present on the usual clone together with CD23?
nodes.note: The common clone has the chronic lymphocytic leukemia phenotype: CD5-positive, CD23-positive, weak CD20 and CD19-positive.

nodes.q: Which B-cell count separates it from chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
nodes.a: Fewer than 5,000 clonal B cells per µL
nodes.note: At 5,000 per µL or more the diagnosis is chronic lymphocytic leukemia; with nodes or spleen enlargement but fewer than 5,000 per µL it is small lymphocytic lymphoma. Below 500 per µL is 'low-count' MBL, which rarely progresses.

nodes.q: How often does a clone progress to a disease needing treatment?
nodes.note: Higher with high B-cell counts.

nodes.q: Even without progression, which complication is more frequent in these patients than in others their age?
nodes.note: Immune function is mildly impaired (lower normal antibody levels); second cancers, especially of the skin, are also a little more common.

nodes.q: What is the management?
nodes.a: Observation with an annual blood count and examination
nodes.note: No treatment is given, and it is not cancer until it progresses.

nodes.q: His lymphocytosis could suggest chronic lymphocytic leukemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **5,000 or more clonal B cells per µL**, smudge cells on the smear; may have enlarged nodes or spleen, anemia or thrombocytopenia
**Fewer than 5,000 per µL, normal blood counts and examination**

nodes.note: The trap: both have the same CD5-positive, CD23-positive kappa-restricted phenotype.

nodes.q: His raised lymphocyte count could be reactive. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Viral infection or stress; **polyclonal cells with a normal kappa-to-lambda ratio**, often atypical lymphocytes
**Skewed kappa-to-lambda ratio in a well person**

nodes.q: His B cells could suggest follicular lymphoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painless lymph nodes + CD10-positive, CD5-negative B cells + t(14;18)**
**CD5-positive, CD10-negative clone, no lymph nodes**

nodes.q: His CD5-positive B cells could suggest mantle cell lymphoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **CD5-positive, CD23-negative, cyclin D1-positive with t(11;14)**; nodes or spleen enlarged
**CD5-positive, CD23-positive, cyclin D1-negative, normal examination**

root.stem: A 67-year-old man has had 3 months of worsening low back pain that is now severe. He is tender over the fifth lumbar vertebra. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL with a normal mean corpuscular volume, serum calcium is 11.6 mg/dL, and creatinine is 2.3 mg/dL. Total serum protein is high while albumin is low, and electrophoresis shows a tall narrow spike of immunoglobulin G. A urine dipstick is negative for protein, but urine electrophoresis shows a band of free light chains. His blood smear shows red cells stacked like rolls of coins. A spine x-ray shows a compression fracture of the fifth lumbar vertebra and an x-ray of the pelvis shows four sharply outlined holes in the iliac crest. A bone marrow biopsy shows sheets of atypical plasma cells with a chromosomal translocation, and chemotherapy including a proteasome inhibitor is started.
root.oneliner: 67M + 3 months of severe low back pain + point tenderness at L5 + anemia, calcium 11.6, creatinine 2.3 + tall IgG spike on electrophoresis + negative urine dipstick but free light chains in urine + stacked red cells + L5 compression fracture and punched-out iliac lesions + marrow sheets of plasma cells with a translocation
highlight: tender over the fifth lumbar vertebra
tall narrow spike of immunoglobulin G
negative for protein, but urine electrophoresis shows a band of free light chains
four sharply outlined holes in the iliac crest
sheets of atypical plasma cells with a chromosomal translocation

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow that make one identical (monoclonal) immunoglobulin. The clincher: **sheets of clonal plasma cells in the marrow + a monoclonal spike in blood or urine + organ damage (high calcium, kidney failure, anemia, lytic bone lesions)**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Same disease; "myelomatosis" is an older term.

nodes.q: Which four-letter acronym lists the organ damage that separates myeloma from a benign plasma cell condition?
nodes.a: CRAB: hypercalcemia (Calcium), Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions
nodes.note: He has all four. Treatment is started when one of these, or another myeloma-defining event, is present.

nodes.q: Which normal cell does the cancer copy?
nodes.a: The plasma cell, a terminally differentiated B cell
nodes.note: Under the microscope the cells have an eccentric nucleus with a clock-face pattern and a clear perinuclear zone. Immunoglobulin G (IgG) is the most common product, then immunoglobulin A (IgA).

nodes.q: In a Southern blot with a probe for the immunoglobulin joining (J) region, his B cells give a 1.5-kb band and his T cells give a 6-kb band. What does the larger band in the T cells mean?
nodes.note: B cells join V, D and J segments, which shortens the fragment; T cells rearrange T cell receptor genes instead, so their immunoglobulin genes stay in germline form. Every myeloma cell carries the same V-D-J rearrangement, which is why the protein is monoclonal.

nodes.q: Which mechanism makes the bone lesions lytic and raises his calcium?
nodes.a: Local release of interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor by the myeloma cells, which activates osteoclasts
nodes.note: Myeloma cells also raise RANKL (receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand) and block osteoblasts through DKK1. Parathyroid hormone is low and parathyroid hormone-related protein is not the cause. Because osteoblasts are not stimulated, the lesions are purely lytic, the bone scan can be falsely negative and alkaline phosphatase stays normal.

nodes.q: What is the most feared consequence of vertebral collapse?
nodes.note: Look for new leg weakness, a sensory level or loss of bladder control.

nodes.q: What is the first step when cord compression is suspected?
nodes.a: High-dose dexamethasone at once, then urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine, followed by radiation or surgery
nodes.note: Bisphosphonates or denosumab are given long term to reduce fractures.

nodes.q: Why is the anemia normocytic?
nodes.a: Plasma cells crowd out the red cell precursors in the marrow
nodes.note: Reduced erythropoietin from kidney damage adds to it. Rouleaux (stacked red cells) form because the excess immunoglobulin coats the cells and removes their charge repulsion.

nodes.q: Why is the urine dipstick negative for protein when so many light chains are in the urine?
nodes.a: The dipstick detects albumin, not free light chains
nodes.note: Free light chains (Bence Jones protein) are found by urine protein electrophoresis or the sulfosalicylic acid test. They are filtered easily because they are small.

nodes.q: Which kidney lesion do the light chains cause?
nodes.note: Light chains bind Tamm-Horsfall protein and form pink, fractured casts in the distal tubules, surrounded by multinucleated giant cells. High calcium and dehydration add to the damage.

nodes.q: Which tests confirm the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, serum free light chains, and a bone marrow biopsy
nodes.note: Marrow plasma cells of 10% or more define the disease. Imaging is a skeletal survey, or better whole-body low-dose computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging.

nodes.q: How does a proteasome inhibitor such as bortezomib kill myeloma cells?
nodes.note: Myeloma cells make huge amounts of immunoglobulin and depend on the proteasome to clear misfolded proteins and to activate nuclear factor kappa B. Blocking it causes toxic protein build-up and cell death. The cells do not stop releasing calcium or become more stable; they die.

nodes.q: What is the usual treatment plan for a fit patient?
nodes.a: A proteasome inhibitor plus lenalidomide and dexamethasone, then autologous stem cell transplant
nodes.note: Anti-CD38 antibodies such as daratumumab are also used. Lenalidomide is teratogenic and raises the risk of venous thrombosis. Bisphosphonates protect the bones.

nodes.q: Despite his high total protein, which kind of bacteria cause the infections that drive much of the early mortality?
nodes.a: Encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae
nodes.note: The clone suppresses normal immunoglobulins, so functional antibody levels are low (immunoparesis) even though total protein is high. Infection and kidney failure are the leading causes of death.

nodes.q: Light chains can also deposit as a different kidney disease with proteinuria and enlarged kidneys. Which?
nodes.note: Light chains misfold into beta-pleated sheets. Congo red staining shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light.

nodes.q: His kidney failure could also come from AL amyloidosis. How do you tell it apart from cast nephropathy?

split.note: **Amorphous pink deposits that stain with Congo red and show apple-green birefringence** in the glomeruli, with enlarged kidneys and heavy proteinuria
**Pink fractured casts in the tubules with giant cells + a negative dipstick for albumin + hypercalcemia**

nodes.note: The trap: both occur with free light chains in the urine.

nodes.q: A monoclonal spike without symptoms could be a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). How do you tell it from his illness?

split.note: **Spike under 3 g/dL + fewer than 10% marrow plasma cells + no CRAB features**; found by chance and followed yearly
**10% or more marrow plasma cells or myeloma-defining organ damage (CRAB)**; this man has fractures, anemia, high calcium and kidney failure

nodes.note: The trap: both have the same kind of monoclonal protein.

nodes.q: A monoclonal protein with anemia could suggest Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Monoclonal immunoglobulin M (IgM) + hyperviscosity (blurred vision, nosebleeds, headaches) + lymphoplasmacytic cells**; no lytic bone lesions
**Monoclonal IgG (or IgA) + punched-out lytic bone lesions + plasma cells in the marrow**

nodes.q: Back pain in an older man with vertebral involvement could be metastatic prostate cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sclerotic (osteoblastic) lesions + high prostate-specific antigen + raised alkaline phosphatase**; no monoclonal spike
**Purely lytic punched-out lesions + monoclonal spike + normal alkaline phosphatase**

nodes.q: A pathologic fracture can have other causes. Which finding points away from each?

**Marrow full of myeloblasts with Auer rods**

root.stem: An 82-year-old man who lives alone has had 2 months of bleeding gums and painful bruises on both legs. His daughter reports that he mostly eats tea, toast and canned soup and has had no fresh fruit or vegetables for a year. His gums are swollen, purple and bleed when touched. On his shins there are small red spots around hair follicles, and the hairs are coiled like corkscrews. An old surgical scar has reopened. His platelet count, prothrombin time, serum folate and vitamin B6 level are normal.
root.oneliner: 82M + lives alone, no fruit or vegetables for a year + bleeding swollen gums + painful bruises + perifollicular hemorrhages with corkscrew hairs + reopened old scar + normal platelets, prothrombin time, folate and vitamin B6
highlight: no fresh fruit or vegetables for a year
swollen, purple and bleed when touched
small red spots around hair follicles
platelet count, prothrombin time, serum folate and vitamin B6 level are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Vitamin C deficiency. The clincher: **swollen bleeding gums + perifollicular hemorrhages with corkscrew hairs in a person with no fruit or vegetables and normal platelets and clotting tests**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Same disease. In infants it is called Barlow disease.

nodes.q: Which step of collagen synthesis fails?
nodes.a: Hydroxylation of selected proline and lysine residues on the pro-alpha chains
nodes.note: This happens in the rough endoplasmic reticulum, before the triple helix forms. Cleavage of the terminal peptides and self-assembly into fibrils come later and are not the defect.

nodes.q: Which enzyme needs vitamin C and is mainly compromised?
nodes.note: Lysyl hydroxylase is also affected. Pyruvate dehydrogenase and pyruvate carboxylase do not depend on vitamin C.

nodes.q: What does vitamin C do for the enzyme?
nodes.a: It keeps the iron in the enzyme's active site in the reduced Fe2+ form
nodes.note: Vitamin C is a reducing agent. It is also needed to absorb dietary iron and for dopamine beta-hydroxylase.

nodes.q: Why do his gums and small vessels bleed?
nodes.a: Under-hydroxylated collagen cannot form a stable triple helix, so the vessel walls and gum connective tissue are weak
nodes.note: Hydroxyproline allows hydrogen bonds that stabilise the helix. Weak collagen also explains the reopened scar and poor wound healing.

nodes.q: Why are his platelet count and prothrombin time normal?
nodes.a: The defect is in the vessel wall, not in platelets or the clotting cascade
nodes.note: Compare vitamin K deficiency, where clotting factors are defective and prothrombin time is prolonged.

nodes.q: Humans cannot make vitamin C. Roughly how long do body stores last once intake stops?
nodes.note: So signs appear after months of no fruit or vegetables. Groups at risk: older people living alone, alcohol use disorder, restrictive diets, malabsorption; smoking raises the requirement.

nodes.q: Which blood count abnormality often accompanies it, from chronic bleeding and poor iron absorption?
nodes.note: It may be normocytic or microcytic; vitamin C is needed to absorb non-heme iron.

nodes.q: Which test confirms it?
nodes.a: Low plasma vitamin C (ascorbic acid) level
nodes.note: Treatment is not delayed to wait for it, because the clinical picture is enough.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Oral vitamin C (ascorbic acid) and a diet with citrus fruit and vegetables
nodes.note: Bleeding and pain improve within days, and gum changes within weeks. Screen for other nutritional deficiencies in a malnourished older person.

nodes.q: In an infant fed only boiled milk, which bone finding is classic?
nodes.a: Subperiosteal hemorrhage with painful legs held in a frog-leg position
nodes.note: X-rays show a white line at the growth plate and a ring around the epiphysis (Wimberger ring).

nodes.q: His bruising could suggest vitamin K deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Prolonged prothrombin time** because factors II, VII, IX and X are not carboxylated; seen with antibiotics, malabsorption or warfarin; no corkscrew hairs
**Normal prothrombin time + swollen gums + perifollicular hemorrhages and corkscrew hairs** in a person with no fresh produce

nodes.note: The trap: both cause bruising in a malnourished older person.

nodes.q: His skin bleeding could suggest thrombocytopenia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low platelet count + petechiae on the legs and mucosal bleeding** with no perifollicular pattern or swollen gums
**Normal platelet count + perifollicular hemorrhages + swollen bleeding gums**

nodes.q: Other causes of poor nutrition or weak connective tissue are possible. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: A lifelong pattern; his problem followed a poor diet

root.stem: A 56-year-old woman has had rheumatoid arthritis for 25 years and has joint pain that has not responded to treatment. She comes for a joint replacement operation and feels tired. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume is 78 fL, leukocyte and platelet counts are normal, and the reticulocyte count is low. Serum iron is 35 µg/dL, total iron-binding capacity is 190 µg/dL (reference 250 to 400), and serum ferritin is 420 ng/mL. A Prussian blue stain of a bone marrow aspirate shows plenty of iron in the macrophages but almost none in the developing red cells.
root.oneliner: 56F + rheumatoid arthritis for 25 years + fatigue + mild microcytic anemia, low reticulocytes + low serum iron + low total iron-binding capacity + high ferritin + marrow Prussian blue: iron in macrophages, little in red cell precursors
highlight: plenty of iron in the macrophages but almost none in the developing red cells

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A mild anemia caused by long-standing inflammation. The clincher: **low serum iron + low total iron-binding capacity + high ferritin, with iron stored in marrow macrophages**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Same condition; the inflammation can be infectious, autoimmune or cancer-related.

nodes.q: Which liver hormone, raised by interleukin-6, causes the iron shortage?
nodes.note: Hepcidin rises with inflammation, so the exam option "decreased hepcidin" is wrong.

nodes.q: Which iron exporter does hepcidin block?
nodes.note: Hepcidin binds ferroportin and makes the cell take it in and degrade it. Iron cannot leave macrophages or be absorbed from the gut.

nodes.q: Where does the iron end up?
nodes.a: Trapped inside macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system
nodes.note: This is why the Prussian blue stain shows abundant macrophage iron but the developing red cells are starved. It is retention, not a lack of uptake. The ferritin is high because it is an acute-phase protein and iron is stored.

nodes.q: Which hormone response is blunted, adding to the low reticulocyte count?
nodes.note: Cytokines blunt the marrow's response to erythropoietin and shorten red cell survival.

nodes.q: Early disease is normocytic. Why is her mean corpuscular volume now slightly low?
nodes.a: After years of restricted iron supply to the marrow, the red cells are made slightly smaller
nodes.note: Early on, the cells are normochromic and normocytic; after years they may become mildly microcytic.

nodes.q: What is the main treatment?
nodes.note: Iron supplements do not help because the iron is trapped, not missing. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents are used in selected cases such as chronic kidney disease or cancer; transfuse if severe.

nodes.q: Which iron test helps to separate it from iron deficiency when the ferritin is borderline?
nodes.a: The soluble transferrin receptor to ferritin ratio (low in chronic disease, high in iron deficiency)
nodes.note: A ferritin under 30 ng/mL means iron deficiency; between 30 and 100 ng/mL the picture may be mixed.

nodes.q: Her microcytic anemia could suggest iron deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low ferritin + high total iron-binding capacity + absent marrow iron stores**; the cause is blood loss or poor intake
**High ferritin + low total iron-binding capacity + iron present in marrow macrophages** with a long inflammatory illness

nodes.note: The trap: both have a low serum iron and a small mean corpuscular volume.

nodes.q: Her low iron with iron seen in the marrow could suggest sideroblastic anemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Ring sideroblasts: Prussian blue shows iron granules circling the nucleus of red cell precursors (iron trapped in mitochondria)**; serum iron and ferritin are high
**Iron lies in macrophages, not in the red cell precursors; serum iron is low**

nodes.q: Other causes of anemia are possible. Which finding in her case rules out each?

Clincher
Missing from her case
rows: **Very high red cell count with target cells + raised hemoglobin A2; normal ferritin and iron**
Normal iron indices; her iron is low and ferritin high
Normal white cell and platelet counts
**Teardrop cells and nucleated red cells on the smear**

root.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought in with a painful, swollen right knee that began 1 week ago after a fall from a low step. In the past 6 months his parents saw red urine twice without pain. He has bruises and growing hematomas on both elbows, and a deep splinter in his palm kept bleeding for hours. His parents and sister are healthy, but his mother's brother needed repeated transfusions as a child. His height and weight are at the 60th percentile. Platelet count, bleeding time and prothrombin time are normal, and the partial thromboplastin time is prolonged.
root.oneliner: 2M + painful swollen knee after minor fall + 2 episodes of painless red urine + bruises and hematomas + prolonged bleeding from a deep splinter + healthy parents, mother's brother needed transfusions + normal platelets, bleeding time and prothrombin time, prolonged partial thromboplastin time
highlight: deep splinter in his palm kept bleeding for hours
Platelet count, bleeding time and prothrombin time are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An inherited X-linked bleeding disorder of the clotting cascade. The clincher: **bleeding into joints and deep tissues in a boy + prolonged partial thromboplastin time with normal prothrombin time, platelet count and bleeding time**. Hemophilia A and B look identical at the bedside.

nodes.q: The exam may list hemophilia B under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Hemophilia A is sometimes called classic hemophilia.

nodes.q: Which form, and which missing factor, is most likely in a boy like him?
nodes.note: About 80 to 85% of hemophilia is type A; type B (factor IX) makes up most of the rest. A clear response to a single injection of factor VIII concentrate would prove it; vitamin K, fibrinogen and folic acid would not help.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern explains an affected boy with healthy parents and a maternal uncle with the same illness?
nodes.note: His mother is a carrier. About one third of cases are new mutations. The factor VIII gene lies on the X chromosome, and an inversion in intron 22 causes many severe cases.

nodes.q: Why is the partial thromboplastin time prolonged while the prothrombin time is normal?
nodes.a: Factors VIII and IX work in the intrinsic pathway, which the partial thromboplastin time measures
nodes.note: Activated factor VIII is the cofactor for factor IXa in activating factor X (the tenase complex). The extrinsic pathway (prothrombin time) bypasses both.

nodes.q: His plasma is mixed 1:1 with normal plasma. What happens to the partial thromboplastin time?
nodes.note: Correction means a missing factor. Failure to correct points to an inhibitor (an antibody against a factor, or a lupus anticoagulant). Factor VIII and IX assays then name the deficient factor.

nodes.q: Why is the bleeding time normal?
nodes.a: The platelet plug forms normally, since platelets and von Willebrand factor are intact
nodes.note: The clot cannot be stabilised by fibrin, so bleeding restarts hours later and into deep tissues.

nodes.q: Suppose his plasma were mixed with plasma from a patient with hemophilia A and the prolonged partial thromboplastin time corrected. Which factor would then be deficient?
nodes.note: Hemophilia A plasma contains factor IX, so it corrects a factor IX deficiency but not a factor VIII deficiency.

nodes.q: Recurrent bleeding into the knee leads to which late joint damage?
nodes.note: Iron from repeated bleeds causes synovitis, cartilage loss and deformity; the knee is the most often affected joint.

nodes.q: Which bleeding site is the most dangerous?
nodes.note: It can follow minor head trauma and is the main cause of death. Bleeding into the muscle can cause compartment syndrome.

nodes.q: Which replacement therapy treats a bleed?
nodes.note: Prophylaxis is given in severe disease. Avoid intramuscular injections, aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Hemophilia B is treated with factor IX concentrate.

nodes.q: Which drug raises factor VIII in mild disease by releasing stored von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from endothelial cells?
nodes.note: It works only in mild hemophilia A, not in hemophilia B. Tranexamic acid helps with mucosal bleeding. Emicizumab (a bispecific antibody that bridges factor IXa and factor X, mimicking factor VIIIa) is used in prophylaxis, especially with inhibitors.

nodes.q: Which complication makes factor replacement stop working?
nodes.note: Detected with a mixing study that fails to correct.

nodes.q: His bleeding and prolonged partial thromboplastin time could suggest von Willebrand disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Mucosal bleeding (nosebleeds, heavy periods) + prolonged bleeding time + abnormal ristocetin test**, autosomal inheritance, both sexes
**Hemarthrosis and deep hematomas in a boy + normal bleeding time**; X-linked

nodes.note: The trap: both reduce factor VIII and prolong the partial thromboplastin time.

nodes.q: Other bleeding disorders are possible. Which finding in his case rules out each?

Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Prolonged prothrombin time first, since factor VII has the shortest half-life**
**Prolonged prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time and bleeding time**
**Both prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time prolonged**

The spleen is not enlarged. Tests for infection, inflammatory disease and cancer are negative, iron studies are normal, and testing for the Philadelphia chromosome is negative. nosebleeds and bruises after minor knocks
white cell count is 8,200/mm3 with a normal differential
Tests for infection, inflammatory disease and cancer are negative
testing for the Philadelphia chromosome is negative

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A myeloproliferative neoplasm in which megakaryocytes overproduce platelets. The clincher: **a persistently very high platelet count with normal hemoglobin and white count, megakaryocyte-rich marrow, no Philadelphia chromosome and no cause for a reactive rise**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Same disease; "essential thrombocytosis" is used too.

nodes.q: Which mutated gene is found in about half of cases?
nodes.note: The usual change is V617F, which keeps the kinase switched on. It is shared with polycythemia vera and primary myelofibrosis. Calreticulin (CALR) and thrombopoietin receptor (MPL) mutations cause most of the rest.

nodes.q: Why is his finger blue and painful although the pulses are full?
nodes.a: Platelet plugs block the small digital arterioles
nodes.note: Large arteries are open; the occlusion is microvascular. It can also appear as burning, red, painful feet (erythromelalgia) or as stroke and venous thrombosis.

nodes.q: Why does he also bleed when his platelet count is so high?
nodes.a: Platelets adsorb large von Willebrand factor multimers (acquired von Willebrand disease) and function abnormally
nodes.note: Bleeding is most likely when the count passes 1,000,000/mm3.

nodes.q: Which workup is needed before the diagnosis can be made?
nodes.a: Excluding reactive causes and other myeloid neoplasms, with testing for the JAK2, CALR and MPL mutations and for the Philadelphia chromosome fusion gene (BCR-ABL1) and a marrow biopsy

nodes.note: An inherited thrombophilia. The clincher: **an unprovoked venous clot in a young person + family history + low protein C activity**.

nodes.note: Protein C, with protein S as its cofactor, cleaves them, so thrombin generation is held in check. Without protein C these factors stay active and the blood clots too easily.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern explains the clot in his mother?

nodes.q: When should protein C activity be measured to avoid a false result?

spleen is felt 9 cm below the left costal margin
teardrops, nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes, but no excess of blasts

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A myeloproliferative neoplasm in which the marrow becomes scarred. The clincher: **teardrop red cells + leukoerythroblastic blood smear + dry tap with marrow fibrosis + large spleen**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?

nodes.note: Older names for the same disease; "idiopathic myelofibrosis" is used too.

nodes.q: Which abnormal cell drives the marrow scarring by releasing growth factors?

nodes.q: Which mutated gene is found in about half to two thirds of cases?

nodes.q: Why is the spleen so large?

nodes.q: What makes the red cells teardrop-shaped?

nodes.q: Why is his uric acid high?

nodes.note: Gout and kidney stones can follow. Weight loss and fatigue come from the same hypermetabolic state.

nodes.q: Which drug shrinks the spleen and relieves his symptoms?

nodes.q: Which fatal transformation occurs in a minority of patients?
nodes.note: Other late events are portal hypertension, thrombosis and splenic infarction.

sharp edges, scattered in the outer parts of both lungs

nodes.q: Which different pattern of spread follows lymphatic channels and gives reticular lines and breathlessness?

nodes.q: How is the primary tumor found?

takes no aspirin or other medicines

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by too little or faulty von Willebrand factor. The clincher: **mucosal bleeding (heavy periods, nosebleeds, bleeding gums) with a prolonged bleeding time, a normal platelet count, low factor VIII and reduced ristocetin-induced aggregation, in both sexes of one family**. A long bleeding time is often the only abnormality; women with mucosal bleeding are the classic case, while boys with joint bleeds suggest hemophilia.

nodes.q: Which platelet aggregation study is reduced in her even though her platelet count is normal?
nodes.note: Ristocetin makes von Willebrand factor bind platelet glycoprotein Ib. With too little or faulty factor, the platelets do not clump.

nodes.q: Which step of platelet plug formation fails when the factor is lacking?
nodes.a: Platelet adhesion to the damaged vessel wall
nodes.note: Von Willebrand factor, made by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes, bridges platelet glycoprotein Ib to exposed subendothelial collagen.

nodes.q: Why are her factor VIII activity low and her partial thromboplastin time long, when the defect is in a platelet-binding protein?
nodes.a: Von Willebrand factor normally carries and protects factor VIII in the blood; without it, factor VIII is cleared quickly
nodes.note: Factor VIII falls only modestly, so the partial thromboplastin time is mildly long and the prothrombin time (extrinsic pathway) is normal.

nodes.q: How is the common form of this disease inherited?
nodes.note: This explains why her father and sister, males and females alike, are affected. Type 1 (partial quantitative deficiency) is the most common; type 2 is a qualitative defect; type 3 is autosomal recessive with near-total absence and bleeds like hemophilia, including into joints.

nodes.q: What explains her mean corpuscular volume of 70 and hemoglobin of 10.5?

nodes.q: Which blood panel confirms the diagnosis?

nodes.q: Which drug releases von Willebrand factor stored in endothelial cells?

nodes.q: Which product is used for severe bleeding, surgery, or when desmopressin fails?
nodes.a: Factor VIII concentrate that contains von Willebrand factor
nodes.note: Tranexamic acid and hormonal contraception also reduce heavy menstrual bleeding.

nodes.q: Her family history could suggest hemophilia A. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **X-linked recessive, so boys; bleeding into joints and muscles; long partial thromboplastin time with a normal bleeding time and a normal ristocetin test**. Hemophilia B (factor IX) looks the same.
**Both sexes; mucosal bleeding with a long bleeding time, low factor VIII and reduced ristocetin aggregation; no joint bleeds**

nodes.note: The trap: both give a low factor VIII and a long partial thromboplastin time.

nodes.q: Her long bleeding time with a normal platelet count could suggest Bernard-Soulier syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Giant platelets with a low count; ristocetin aggregation absent and not corrected by adding normal plasma** (glycoprotein Ib-IX-V missing)
**Normal-sized platelets and count; the ristocetin defect is corrected by adding normal plasma**; factor VIII low

nodes.q: Her easy bleeding could suggest immune thrombocytopenia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low platelet count with petechiae and purpura**; normal factor VIII and ristocetin test
**Normal platelet count; long bleeding time, low factor VIII, reduced ristocetin aggregation**

nodes.q: Her long bleeding time could suggest aspirin use. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Drug history; irreversible cyclooxygenase-1 block with a normal partial thromboplastin time, normal factor VIII and normal ristocetin response**; not lifelong or familial
**Lifelong bleeding since menarche, a family history, low factor VIII and reduced ristocetin response; takes no aspirin**

nodes.q: Her bleeding and anemia could suggest thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low platelets, hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, fever, confusion and kidney injury** (ADAMTS13 deficiency); normal prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times
**Normal platelet count, no schistocytes, no fever or confusion**; the mild anemia is from iron deficiency

nodes.q: Her bleeding could suggest vitamin K deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Long prothrombin time first (factor VII has the shortest half-life), then a long partial thromboplastin time**; normal bleeding time; fat malabsorption, antibiotics or warfarin
**Normal prothrombin time with a long bleeding time**; lifelong and familial

nodes.q: Her prolonged bleeding after a cut could suggest afibrinogenemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **No fibrinogen: long prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time and thrombin time; bleeding from the umbilical stump at birth**; autosomal recessive
**Normal prothrombin time, only a mildly long partial thromboplastin time, and a reduced ristocetin response**; autosomal dominant

split.note: **Acute illness (sepsis, trauma, obstetric): low platelets, long prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer**
**Lifelong, otherwise well; normal platelets and prothrombin time**

root.stem: A 61-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes for follow-up. He has a chronic cough, and his face looks ruddy. Oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. His spleen is not palpable, he has no itching after hot showers, and his skin is not bronze. Hemoglobin is 18.7 g/dL and hematocrit is 56%, with a normal white cell count, a normal platelet count and no immature or teardrop-shaped cells. A peripheral smear shows closely packed red cells of normal shape and size. Serum erythropoietin level is high, and ferritin and transferrin saturation are normal.

highlight: Oxygen saturation is 86% on room air
closely packed red cells of normal shape and size
ferritin and transferrin saturation are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Secondary polycythemia due to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
nodes.note: Too many red cells because the body is responding to something else, here chronic low oxygen. The clincher: **high hemoglobin with chronic hypoxemia and a high erythropoietin level**, while the white cells and platelets are normal.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Polycythemia and erythrocytosis both mean too many red cells; "secondary" separates it from the marrow disease polycythemia vera.

nodes.q: Which hormone, released in response to low oxygen, drives the rise in red cells?
nodes.note: Peritubular cells in the kidney sense hypoxia through hypoxia-inducible factor and release erythropoietin; the marrow then makes more red cells.

nodes.q: Which kidney cancer can raise the hemoglobin in the same way without any hypoxia?
nodes.note: Other erythropoietin-secreting tumors: hepatocellular carcinoma, cerebellar hemangioblastoma (von Hippel-Lindau), leiomyoma and pheochromocytoma. Smokers also raise red cell mass through carbon monoxide. Dehydration gives a relative polycythemia with a normal red cell mass.

nodes.q: Which blood cell line is increased in him?
nodes.a: Red cells only (erythrocytosis); white cells and platelets are normal
nodes.note: The smear shows closely packed red cells of normal shape and size. A rise in only the red cell line points to a reactive cause rather than a marrow disease of all three lines.

nodes.q: Which property of blood rises with his hematocrit and raises his risk of stroke and clots?
nodes.note: Viscosity climbs steeply once the hematocrit passes about 55%, slowing flow and causing headache, dizziness and thrombosis.

nodes.q: Which long-term treatment corrects the cause of his high red cell mass?
nodes.note: Raising oxygen saturation removes the stimulus for erythropoietin. Stop smoking (carbon monoxide also stimulates red cell production). Phlebotomy is kept for symptoms of hyperviscosity with a very high hematocrit.

nodes.q: His high hemoglobin could suggest polycythemia vera. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low erythropoietin, JAK2 mutation, itching after hot showers, enlarged spleen, often high white cells and platelets**; normal oxygen saturation
**High erythropoietin with low oxygen saturation**; normal white cells and platelets; spleen not palpable

nodes.note: The trap: both raise hemoglobin and hematocrit.

nodes.q: His ruddy face could suggest hereditary hemochromatosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bronze skin, diabetes, cirrhosis, arthropathy; high ferritin and transferrin saturation**; hemoglobin usually normal
**Normal ferritin and transferrin saturation; high hemoglobin from hypoxia**

nodes.q: Could hypersplenism explain his blood count? How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Enlarged spleen with low counts (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia)**
**High hemoglobin; spleen not palpable; normal white cells and platelets**

nodes.q: Could myelodysplastic syndrome explain his blood count? How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low counts with dysplastic cells (macrocytosis, ring sideroblasts, hypogranular neutrophils) in an older adult**
**High, not low, hemoglobin; normal-looking cells**

nodes.q: Could agnogenic myeloid metaplasia (primary myelofibrosis) explain his blood count? How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Teardrop cells and immature cells on the smear, a large spleen, marrow fibrosis with a dry tap**; anemia is typical
**Packed normal-shaped red cells; no immature cells; spleen not palpable**

tender 2-cm swelling over the back of his head
drinks a lot of water and urinates often
no itching, no family history of eczema or asthma

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A clonal growth of Langerhans-type dendritic cells that can involve skin, bone, liver, spleen and pituitary. The clincher: **CD1a-positive cells with grooved nuclei and tennis racket-shaped Birbeck granules, in a child with a seborrheic-like rash, lytic skull lesions and organ enlargement**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The older name. The severe infant form is Letterer-Siwe disease, and the single bone lesion form is eosinophilic granuloma.

nodes.q: From which cell type do the abnormal cells derive?
nodes.a: Dendritic cells (Langerhans cells, the antigen-presenting cells of the skin)
nodes.note: Bone-marrow-derived cells that normally present antigen in the epidermis.

nodes.q: Which structure seen on electron microscopy is the hallmark of these cells?
nodes.note: Rod-shaped with a clear bulb at one end, like a tennis racket; they contain langerin.

nodes.q: Which surface marker on these cells is used to confirm the diagnosis on immunohistochemistry?
nodes.note: The cells also stain for S100 and langerin.

nodes.q: What do the cells and their neighbors look like under the light microscope?
nodes.a: Large cells with grooved, coffee-bean-shaped nuclei mixed with eosinophils
nodes.note: The eosinophils give the single bone form its name, eosinophilic granuloma.

nodes.q: Which mutated gene in the mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway is found in about half of cases?
nodes.note: This shows the disease is a clonal neoplasm of the myeloid dendritic lineage and not a reactive process.

nodes.q: What explains his thirst and frequent urination?
nodes.a: Central diabetes insipidus from infiltration of the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary
nodes.note: Lack of antidiuretic hormone gives large volumes of dilute urine. Lytic skull lesions + diabetes insipidus + bulging eyes (exophthalmos) form the classic Hand-Schüller-Christian triad; the skin rash, organ enlargement and young age here lean toward multisystem disease (the severe infant form is Letterer-Siwe).

nodes.q: Which drug combination treats multisystem disease?
nodes.note: A single bone lesion is treated by curettage or observation and often regresses.

nodes.q: His scalp rash could suggest seborrheic dermatitis. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A lymphoma of B-cell origin in which a few large malignant cells sit in a sea of reactive inflammatory cells. The clincher: **large binucleate 'owl-eye' cells that are CD15 and CD30 positive and CD20 negative, scattered among small lymphocytes, eosinophils and plasma cells**, in a teenager with neck and mediastinal nodes and B symptoms.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The older name for the same disease.

nodes.q: What are the large binucleate cells called?
nodes.note: Derived from germinal-center B cells that have lost most B-cell markers. They are rare (often under 1% of the cells); the reactive cells around them make up most of the mass, and cytokines cause the fever and sweats.

nodes.q: Which two markers on these cells define the classical form?
nodes.note: CD20 (a B-cell marker) is usually negative in the classical form, unlike most B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

nodes.q: Which histologic subtype fits a teenager with a mediastinal mass, collagen bands and large cells sitting in clear spaces?
nodes.note: The most common subtype (about 70%). The cells in clear spaces are lacunar cells, a Reed-Sternberg variant whose cytoplasm shrinks away during fixation. Typical of adolescents and young adults, slightly more often women, with mediastinal involvement and an excellent prognosis.

nodes.q: Which named group of his symptoms carries a worse prognosis and raises his stage letter from A to B?
nodes.a: B symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats and weight loss)
nodes.note: Fever above 38°C, drenching night sweats and loss of more than 10% of body weight in 6 months. His generalized itching and node pain after alcohol are classic for Hodgkin lymphoma but are not B symptoms.

nodes.q: Which virus, linked to his illness 3 years ago, is found inside the malignant cells in many cases?
nodes.note: Found in up to 40% of classical cases overall and most often in the mixed cellularity subtype and in people with human immunodeficiency virus infection. A past history of infectious mononucleosis raises the risk.

nodes.q: Which cytokine made by the malignant cells draws the eosinophils into his node?
nodes.note: Interleukin-5 recruits and activates eosinophils; other cytokines (interleukin-13, transforming growth factor beta) drive the fibrosis and the reactive background.

nodes.q: How does this lymphoma typically spread from his neck nodes to his chest?
nodes.a: Contiguously, from one lymph node group to the next neighboring group
nodes.note: That is why involvement is often localized (neck plus mediastinum) and extranodal spread is uncommon. It also makes radiation fields predictable.

nodes.q: What is the age distribution of this lymphoma?
nodes.a: Bimodal: a peak in young adults (about 15 to 35) and a second peak after about 55
nodes.note: Non-Hodgkin lymphomas, by contrast, rise steadily with age (apart from Burkitt and lymphoblastic lymphoma in children).

nodes.q: What explains his puffy face and neck and the distended veins over his upper chest?

nodes.note: Blood from the head and arms cannot drain into the right atrium; symptoms worsen lying flat or bending forward. Severe cases cause raised intracranial pressure and airway swelling; it is an oncologic emergency.

nodes.q: Which hormone can the tumor cells make that raises the blood calcium?

nodes.q: What explains his shortness of breath when he lies flat?

nodes.note: Lying flat lets the mass press more on the trachea and large vessels.

nodes.q: Which imaging study is used for staging?

nodes.note: Staging uses the Ann Arbor system, with the A or B suffix for symptoms.

nodes.q: Which chemotherapy regimen is standard?
nodes.note: Radiation is added for bulky mediastinal disease. Brentuximab vedotin (an anti-CD30 antibody–drug conjugate) and checkpoint inhibitors are used in advanced or relapsed disease.

nodes.q: Which drug in this regimen causes pulmonary fibrosis?
nodes.note: Free-radical lung injury; avoid high-concentration oxygen.

nodes.q: Which drug in this regimen can damage the heart muscle years later?
nodes.note: Dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy from free radicals; dexrazoxane, an iron chelator, protects the heart. Chest radiation adds coronary disease, and survivors also face second cancers (breast, lung, thyroid, acute myeloid leukemia).

nodes.q: What does his two-gene deletion cause?
nodes.a: Alpha-thalassemia trait: mild microcytic anemia with normal iron stores
nodes.note: Often mistaken for iron deficiency. Red cell count is high for the anemia.

nodes.q: His two deletions sit on different chromosomes. What is that arrangement called?
nodes.note: Common in people of African ancestry. The alternative, both deletions on one chromosome, is cis (--/αα).

nodes.a: Antibody screen and crossmatch before each transfusion, using records of past antibodies

nodes.note: The trap: both have a positive direct antiglobulin test and reticulocytosis.

**Symptoms after 3 to 14 days, no reaction during the transfusion** (IgG memory response); extravascular

**Jaundice and anemia in the mother after her own transfusion**

**Recent transfusion + new alloantibody + positive direct antiglobulin test**
