root.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had 4 months of tiredness, night sweats and a feeling of fullness in the left upper abdomen after small meals. She also bruises easily. Her spleen tip is felt 6 cm below the left costal margin. Her white blood cell count is 128,000/mm3 with neutrophils at every stage of maturity, including myelocytes and metamyelocytes, and 6% basophils. Her hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL, her platelet count is 480,000/mm3 and blast cells make up 2% of the white cells. A leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score is low. Genetic testing shows a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22.
root.oneliner: 52F + 4 months of fatigue, night sweats and early satiety + bruising + spleen 6 cm below the left costal margin + white blood cell count 128,000 with all stages of neutrophil maturation + 6% basophils + 2% blasts + low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase + translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22
highlight: fullness in the left upper abdomen after small meals
6 cm below the left costal margin
neutrophils at every stage of maturity

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A cancer of marrow stem cells with massive overproduction of maturing granulocytes. The clincher: **very high white count with every stage of granulocyte maturation, basophilia, big spleen and a low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score**, proven by the 9;22 translocation.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which group of marrow disorders does it belong to?
nodes.note: Clonal stem cell disorders with too many maturing myeloid cells; the others are polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis, which carry JAK2 mutations instead of the 9;22 translocation.

nodes.q: What is the shortened chromosome 22 made by her translocation called?
nodes.note: A reciprocal translocation t(9;22), not a point mutation; present in almost all cases.

nodes.q: Which two genes does it fuse?
nodes.a: BCR on chromosome 22 with ABL1 on chromosome 9 (BCR-ABL1)
nodes.note: Neither gene carries a point mutation; the new fusion gene is the problem.

nodes.q: What does the fusion protein do to the cell?
nodes.a: It is a constitutively active non-receptor tyrosine kinase that drives cell division and blocks apoptosis
nodes.note: The kinase signals continuously without growth factor, so cell-cycle progression is pushed on and programmed death is suppressed.

nodes.q: Which drug blocks the fusion kinase?
nodes.note: A tyrosine kinase inhibitor that occupies the adenosine triphosphate site of the kinase. Dasatinib and nilotinib are alternatives; a gatekeeper T315I mutation causes resistance.

nodes.q: How is the response to treatment followed?
nodes.a: Quantitative polymerase chain reaction for BCR-ABL1 transcripts in the blood
nodes.note: Falling transcript levels mark a molecular response; a rise suggests resistance or poor adherence.

nodes.q: In which phase is the disease usually found at diagnosis?
nodes.note: Often found by chance on a routine blood count. Untreated, it progresses over years through an accelerated phase.

nodes.q: What aggressive stage follows, with 20% or more blasts?
nodes.note: The disease behaves like acute leukemia, usually myeloid but sometimes lymphoid, with fever, bone pain, bleeding and a rising white count.

nodes.q: Cells in blast crisis often survive combination chemotherapy, with undetectable drug inside them. Which mechanism explains this?
nodes.a: Overexpression of the P-glycoprotein drug efflux pump (multidrug resistance protein 1)
nodes.note: An adenosine triphosphate-driven pump moves drugs such as mitoxantrone and vinblastine out of the cell faster than they enter.

nodes.q: Her high white count could be a leukemoid reaction to an infection. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score + toxic granulation and Döhle bodies**; an infection is present; no basophilia, no big spleen, no Philadelphia chromosome
**Low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score + basophilia + splenomegaly + Philadelphia chromosome**

nodes.note: The trap: both give a very high white count with a left shift.

nodes.q: Acute myeloid leukemia can also raise the white count with a bruising tendency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **20% or more myeloblasts, Auer rods, anemia and thrombocytopenia** with few maturing cells in between; abrupt onset
**Maturing granulocytes at every stage, few blasts, high platelets and a big spleen**; slow onset

nodes.q: Primary myelofibrosis also gives a big spleen. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Teardrop cells, nucleated red cells, dry marrow tap with fibrosis, JAK2 mutation**; no Philadelphia chromosome
**Philadelphia chromosome + basophilia + marrow full of maturing granulocytes**

nodes.q: Her high white count at middle age could suggest chronic lymphocytic leukemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small mature lymphocytes with smudge cells**, lymph node enlargement
**Granulocytes at all stages of maturity**, big spleen, Philadelphia chromosome

root.stem: A 6-year-old girl has been pale and mildly yellow since early infancy, with repeated tiredness and one gallstone found on ultrasound. Her spleen is enlarged. Her hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, reticulocytes are 12%, and indirect bilirubin is raised. The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative and osmotic fragility is normal. A blood smear shows red cells with small regular spikes and no spherocytes or Heinz bodies. Her parents are healthy and a younger brother has the same condition. Her symptoms do not follow any drug or food.
root.oneliner: 6F + pale and mildly yellow since early infancy + gallstone + splenomegaly + hemoglobin 7.8, reticulocytes 12%, raised indirect bilirubin + negative Coombs test + normal osmotic fragility + spiked red cells, no spherocytes or Heinz bodies + healthy parents, affected brother + no drug or food trigger
highlight: test is negative and osmotic fragility is normal
parents are healthy and a younger brother has the same condition
do not follow any drug or food

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The second most common inherited red cell enzyme defect. The clincher: **chronic hemolysis from infancy + negative Coombs test + spiked (burr) red cells + normal osmotic fragility + no oxidant trigger**.

nodes.q: Which metabolic step is blocked?
nodes.a: The last step of glycolysis, phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate
nodes.note: This step makes net adenosine triphosphate (ATP) by substrate-level phosphorylation. Red cells have no mitochondria, so glycolysis is their only energy source.

nodes.q: What is the main consequence for the red cell?
nodes.note: Without ATP the membrane ion pumps fail, the cell loses potassium and water, becomes rigid and spiky, and is destroyed in the spleen. Liver cells make another form of the enzyme and cope better.

nodes.q: Which glycolytic intermediate builds up behind the block and shifts her oxygen curve to the right?
nodes.note: The right shift releases oxygen more easily, so patients tolerate their anemia better than expected.

nodes.q: On a graph of enzyme activity against phosphoenolpyruvate, her curve reaches the same maximum as normal but needs more substrate. Which enzyme change explains this?
nodes.a: A mutation that increases the Michaelis constant (Km), lowering substrate affinity
nodes.note: The maximum velocity is unchanged, so it is not less enzyme made, faster breakdown or a noncompetitive inhibitor; those would lower the maximum.

nodes.q: How is it inherited?
nodes.note: Parents are healthy carriers; siblings are affected, as with her brother.

nodes.q: Which red cell shape is typical on the smear?
nodes.note: Evenly spaced short spikes, unlike the irregular spikes of acanthocytes. Splenectomy raises the count of these cells.

nodes.q: Which complication of chronic hemolysis shows on her ultrasound?
nodes.note: Excess bilirubin from red cell breakdown forms calcium bilirubinate stones.

nodes.q: Which virus can suddenly stop red cell production and cause an aplastic crisis?
nodes.note: It infects red cell precursors; a patient with chronic hemolysis has no reserve, so the hemoglobin drops fast.

nodes.q: What is the treatment for severe disease?
nodes.note: Splenectomy reduces hemolysis without curing it. Give folic acid. The activator mitapivat is a newer option.

nodes.q: Her inherited hemolysis with a negative Coombs test could suggest glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Episodic hemolysis after oxidants such as primaquine or fava beans, Heinz bodies and bite cells**; X-linked
**Chronic hemolysis from infancy, burr cells, no oxidant trigger**; autosomal recessive

nodes.note: The trap: both are inherited enzyme defects with a negative Coombs test.

nodes.q: Her anemia, jaundice, gallstone and big spleen could suggest hereditary spherocytosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Spherocytes without central pallor, high mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, abnormal osmotic fragility or eosin-5-maleimide test, autosomal dominant**
**Spiked burr cells with normal osmotic fragility; autosomal recessive**

root.stem: A 66-year-old man has had 5 days of fever, productive cough and sharp right-sided chest pain on breathing in. His temperature is 38.9°C and he has crackles and dullness over the right lower chest. A chest x-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation, and a sputum Gram stain shows many neutrophils with gram-positive diplococci. His white blood cell count is 54,000/mm3 with segmented neutrophils, 12% band forms and a few metamyelocytes; the neutrophils show toxic granulation and Döhle bodies, and there are no blasts. His hemoglobin is 14 g/dL, his platelet count is 460,000/mm3, and his spleen is not enlarged.
root.oneliner: 66M + 5 days of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain + right lower lobe consolidation + gram-positive diplococci on sputum Gram stain + white blood cell count 54,000 with band forms, a few metamyelocytes, toxic granulation and Döhle bodies, no blasts + platelets 460,000 + normal hemoglobin + no splenomegaly

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A very high white count (often above 50,000/mm3) from a non-leukemic cause, here pneumonia. The clincher: **marked neutrophilia with left shift, toxic granulation and Döhle bodies, no blasts, a raised leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score, and a clear infection**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both terms mean a benign marrow response of mature and slightly immature neutrophils to infection or inflammation.

nodes.q: Which signals make the marrow release so many neutrophils and band forms?
nodes.a: Cytokines such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor
nodes.note: Release of stored neutrophils, including band forms and a few metamyelocytes, is called a left shift.

nodes.q: Which neutrophil enzyme score is raised in this condition?
nodes.note: Reactive neutrophils are rich in the enzyme; neoplastic neutrophils of chronic myeloid leukemia are not.

nodes.q: Which neutrophil changes on the smear point to infection?
nodes.a: Toxic granulation, Döhle bodies and cytoplasmic vacuoles
nodes.note: Döhle bodies are blue patches of leftover ribosomal RNA in the cytoplasm.

nodes.q: Which organism most likely caused his pneumonia?
nodes.note: Lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci, alpha-hemolytic, with a polysaccharide capsule; sensitive to optochin and soluble in bile.

nodes.q: How is it managed?
nodes.note: The count falls as the infection clears; no leukemia work-up or treatment is needed unless it persists.

nodes.q: His high count could suggest chronic myeloid leukemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score + basophilia + big spleen + Philadelphia chromosome**; no infection needed
**High leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score + toxic granulation + an infection + no basophilia, no splenomegaly, no Philadelphia chromosome**

nodes.note: The trap: both show a very high white count with a left shift and immature granulocytes.

nodes.q: His fever and very high white count could suggest an acute leukemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **20% or more blasts, anemia and low platelets**, a gap with few maturing cells in between
**No blasts, a smooth range from bands to segmented neutrophils, normal hemoglobin and raised platelets**

nodes.q: His platelet count of 460,000 could suggest essential thrombocythemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Persistently high platelets without a cause + JAK2, CALR or MPL mutation + large marrow megakaryocytes**; white count is near normal
**Platelets rise only with the infection (reactive, driven by interleukin-6) and fall as it clears; white count very high with left shift**

nodes.q: His fever and very high white count could suggest infectious mononucleosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, sore throat, lymph node swelling and a positive heterophile antibody test**
**Neutrophils and bands predominate, with lobar pneumonia and toxic changes**

root.stem: A 6-year-old girl had her spleen removed 18 months ago after a bicycle handlebar injury. She received no vaccines or antibiotics afterwards. She now has one day of fever to 40°C, chills, vomiting and drowsiness, and her blood pressure is 78/42 mm Hg with scattered petechiae. Her platelet count is 520,000/mm3. Her lymphocyte count is normal. A blood smear shows red cells containing a single small round dark purple dot and some target cells.
root.oneliner: 6F + spleen removed 18 months ago after trauma, no vaccines or antibiotic prophylaxis + 1 day of fever 40°C, chills, vomiting, drowsiness + hypotension and petechiae + platelets 520,000 + normal lymphocyte count + red cells with a single small round dark purple dot and target cells
highlight: single small round dark purple dot

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Asplenia (post-splenectomy state) with overwhelming post-splenectomy infection
nodes.note: No spleen means loss of the filter that clears blood-borne bacteria. The clincher: **prior splenectomy + Howell-Jolly bodies on smear + sudden fulminant sepsis**.

nodes.q: Which kind of infection is the key lifelong risk of having no spleen?
nodes.note: Risk is highest in young children and in the first years, but persists for life.

nodes.q: Which organism causes most of these infections?
nodes.note: Next are Haemophilus influenzae type b and Neisseria meningitidis (mnemonic: SHiN). Salmonella, Babesia and Capnocytophaga can also cause severe disease.

nodes.q: Why does losing the spleen leave her open to encapsulated bacteria?
nodes.a: Splenic macrophages normally clear bacteria coated with antibody and complement (opsonized), and the spleen helps make the early antibody response to capsular polysaccharides
nodes.note: Without it, bacteria multiply in the blood unchecked, and sepsis can progress within hours.

nodes.q: What are the dark dots inside her red cells?
nodes.note: The spleen normally pits these out; target cells and acanthocytes also appear.

nodes.q: Which blood count change follows splenectomy within weeks?
nodes.note: Platelets are no longer pooled in the spleen. Low platelets suggest a large spleen, not an absent one.

nodes.q: Which vaccines should be given before elective splenectomy, ideally at least 2 weeks earlier?
nodes.a: Pneumococcal, Haemophilus influenzae type b and meningococcal vaccines
nodes.note: Give them after emergency splenectomy once she is stable, usually 2 weeks later.

nodes.q: Which long-term prophylaxis is given to young children without a spleen?
nodes.note: Usually continued at least until age 5, and for 1 year or more after splenectomy in older patients.

nodes.q: What is the emergency management of her fever?
nodes.a: Blood cultures and immediate intravenous ceftriaxone, with vancomycin added
nodes.note: Do not wait for culture results; mortality rises with each hour of delay.

nodes.q: Her platelet count could raise a question about hypersplenism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Enlarged spleen with low platelets, white cells and red cells (cells trapped in the spleen)**
**No spleen, high platelets, Howell-Jolly bodies, and risk of fulminant sepsis**

nodes.note: The trap: both involve the spleen, but they push the platelet count in opposite directions.

nodes.q: Her severe infection could instead suggest a T-cell deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low lymphocyte count; opportunistic infections such as cytomegalovirus, Pneumocystis and fungi**
**Normal lymphocyte count; sudden sepsis from encapsulated bacteria + Howell-Jolly bodies**

nodes.q: Her Howell-Jolly bodies could suggest sickle cell disease, where the spleen stops working. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sickled cells, painful crises, dactylitis and hemolytic anemia**; the spleen scars from repeated infarcts (autosplenectomy)
**Previously healthy child, spleen removed after trauma**; normal hemoglobin

root.stem: A 34-year-old woman has had 2 weeks of tiredness, bleeding gums and easy bruising. She has pallor, scattered petechiae and large bruises on her legs, and she bled for a long time after a dental extraction last week. Her white blood cell count is 36,000/mm3, hemoglobin 8 g/dL and platelet count 25,000/mm3. The smear shows 80% abnormal cells with heavy granules and bundles of needle-shaped inclusions inside them. Prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time are prolonged, fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is high. Cytogenetic testing of the abnormal cells is sent.
root.oneliner: 34F + 2 weeks of fatigue, bleeding gums and bruising + petechiae + prolonged bleeding after dental extraction + white blood cell count 36,000, hemoglobin 8, platelets 25,000 + 80% granulated abnormal cells with bundles of needle-shaped inclusions + prolonged PT and PTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer
highlight: bled for a long time after a dental extraction
fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is high

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A subtype of acute myeloid leukemia in which cells stall at the promyelocyte stage. The clincher: **abnormal promyelocytes with heavy granules and bundles of Auer rods (faggot cells) + bleeding from disseminated intravascular coagulation** in a young adult.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.a: Acute myeloid leukemia subtype M3 (French-American-British classification)
nodes.note: The same disease under the older classification.

nodes.q: Which enzyme stain is positive in the needle-shaped inclusions?
nodes.note: The inclusions are Auer rods, fused azurophilic granules, a marker of myeloid (not lymphoid) blasts.

nodes.q: Which chromosomal translocation will the cytogenetic test most likely show?
nodes.note: A reciprocal translocation present in virtually all cases and used to confirm the diagnosis.

nodes.q: Which two genes does it fuse?
nodes.a: The promyelocytic leukemia gene (PML) on chromosome 15 and the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene (RARA) on chromosome 17
nodes.note: Polymerase chain reaction for PML-RARA transcripts confirms it and is used to follow treatment.

nodes.q: How does the fusion protein block differentiation?
nodes.a: It binds corepressors that recruit histone deacetylase to retinoic acid response elements, silencing genes needed for maturation
nodes.note: The cells stay frozen at the promyelocyte stage and keep dividing.

nodes.q: Which drug reverses this block?
nodes.note: It binds the receptor, releases the corepressor and recruits coactivators, so the cells mature into neutrophils and die.

nodes.q: Which enzyme activity increases at the gene promoters as retinoic acid binds, relieving the silencing?
nodes.note: Acetylation loosens chromatin so transcription can proceed, in place of the histone deacetylase held there by the fusion protein.

nodes.q: Which second drug is combined with it and degrades the fusion protein?
nodes.note: The combination of retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide gives cure rates above 90% without conventional chemotherapy.

nodes.q: Which complication causes most early deaths?
nodes.a: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) with bleeding, especially into the brain
nodes.note: Granules release tissue factor and other procoagulants, so clotting factors and fibrinogen are consumed.

nodes.q: When should retinoic acid be started?
nodes.a: As soon as the diagnosis is suspected, before genetic confirmation
nodes.note: The bleeding risk is so high that waiting is dangerous; give platelets for the low count and cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen up.

nodes.q: Which complication, with fever, shortness of breath, edema and lung infiltrates, can appear days to weeks into treatment?
nodes.note: Also called retinoic acid syndrome. Caused by cytokines released by maturing cells; arsenic trioxide can cause it too.

nodes.q: How is it treated?
nodes.a: Dexamethasone, with interruption of retinoic acid if severe

nodes.q: Her pallor, bruising and high white count could suggest acute lymphoblastic leukemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lymphoblasts with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase and no Auer rods**, mainly children, often a mediastinal mass or lymph nodes
**Granulated promyelocytes with Auer rods and disseminated intravascular coagulation**

nodes.q: Her gum problems could suggest acute monocytic leukemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Swollen gums from leukemic infiltration**, skin infiltrates and central nervous system disease; monoblasts that stain for nonspecific esterase
**Bleeding gums from disseminated intravascular coagulation + abnormal promyelocytes with bundles of Auer rods**

nodes.note: The trap: both are acute myeloid leukemias with gum findings, but monocytic leukemia infiltrates and swells the gums while promyelocytic leukemia makes them bleed.

root.stem: A 72-year-old man has had 8 months of stiff, painful joints in his hands and knees, and is otherwise well. His hematocrit is 41% and his calcium and creatinine are normal. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a single narrow spike of immunoglobulin G of 1.6 g/dL, with normal immunoglobulin A and M levels. His urine contains no Bence Jones protein, and a skeletal survey shows no bone lesions. A bone marrow biopsy shows 4% plasma cells and no other abnormality.
root.oneliner: 72M + 8 months of stiff painful joints in hands and knees + hematocrit 41%, normal calcium and creatinine + single narrow immunoglobulin G spike 1.6 g/dL + normal immunoglobulin A and M + no Bence Jones protein + no bone lesions + 4% marrow plasma cells
highlight: single narrow spike of immunoglobulin G of 1.6 g/dL
normal immunoglobulin A and M levels

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A premalignant clone of plasma cells that makes a small amount of one immunoglobulin, seen as a monoclonal (M) spike. The clincher: **an M spike under 3 g/dL + under 10% marrow plasma cells + no end-organ damage (no calcium, kidney, anemia or bone problems)**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Same disease; the older wording uses 'uncertain'.

nodes.q: Which cell makes the spike, and which immunoglobulin class is most often involved?
nodes.a: A clonal plasma cell; immunoglobulin G
nodes.note: Every cell of the clone makes the same heavy and light chain, giving one narrow band instead of a broad smear.

nodes.q: Which group of organ-damage findings defines myeloma and is missing here?
nodes.a: Hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia and bone lesions (CRAB)
nodes.note: His calcium, creatinine and hematocrit are normal, the survey is clear and there is no urine light chain.

nodes.q: Below what percentage of marrow plasma cells must the count stay for this diagnosis?
nodes.note: His 4% fits. Ten percent or more, or a plasmacytoma, moves the diagnosis toward myeloma.

nodes.q: How common is it in older adults?
nodes.a: About 3% of people over age 50, rising with age
nodes.note: Usually found by chance during a work-up for another problem; his joint symptoms are unrelated.

nodes.q: At what yearly rate does it progress to a malignant plasma cell or lymphoid disorder, mostly multiple myeloma?
nodes.note: It can also lead to Waldenström macroglobulinemia or light chain amyloidosis.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the clonal immunoglobulin type?
nodes.a: Serum immunofixation (with a free light chain assay)
nodes.note: Electrophoresis finds the spike; immunofixation names the heavy and light chain.

nodes.q: Which findings put him at higher risk of progression?
nodes.a: A spike of 1.5 g/dL or more, a non-immunoglobulin G class, and an abnormal free light chain ratio
nodes.note: The more of these present, the higher the risk.

nodes.q: What is the management?
nodes.a: Observation with repeat protein electrophoresis at about 6 months, then yearly
nodes.note: No treatment is given, and a bone marrow biopsy is needed only if he is high-risk or a new problem arises.

nodes.q: His joint inflammation could suggest that chronic inflammation is raising his immunoglobulin G. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Broad polyclonal band (diffuse hypergammaglobulinemia)** on electrophoresis
**One narrow M spike in the gamma region, with a normal marrow**

nodes.note: The trap: both raise the serum immunoglobulin G level.

nodes.q: Multiple myeloma also gives an immunoglobulin G spike in older adults. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **10% or more marrow plasma cells, Bence Jones proteinuria, lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, renal failure or anemia**
**Marrow plasma cells under 10%, M spike under 3 g/dL, no end-organ damage**

nodes.q: Waldenström macroglobulinemia also shows a monoclonal spike. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Immunoglobulin M spike with hyperviscosity (headache, blurred vision, nosebleeds) and lymphoplasmacytic marrow infiltration**
**Immunoglobulin G spike of 1.6 g/dL, no symptoms of hyperviscosity, 4% plasma cells**

root.stem: A 27-year-old woman has had easy bruising and bleeding from her gums for 2 days. She had a viral respiratory illness 3 weeks ago, eats a varied diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables, takes no medications, and has never had abnormal bleeding before; no one in her family bleeds easily. She is afebrile and alert. Pinpoint red spots and flat purple patches cover both feet and legs. Her spleen is not palpable. Her hemoglobin, leukocyte count and creatinine are normal, her platelet count is 9,000/mm3, and her prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time are normal. The blood smear shows a few slightly enlarged platelets and no fragmented red cells.

highlight: no one in her family bleeds easily
Pinpoint red spots and flat purple patches
hemoglobin, leukocyte count and creatinine are normal
prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Antibodies destroy the platelets. The clincher: **isolated low platelets with a normal prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) in an otherwise well patient who has petechiae and mucosal bleeding**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.a: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (older name: idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura)
nodes.note: All three names describe the same disease; exam options often use the 'purpura' name.

nodes.q: Which event often comes 1 to 3 weeks before the bleeding?
nodes.note: The virus triggers antibodies that also bind platelets. Other triggers and associations: HIV, hepatitis C, systemic lupus erythematosus, chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

nodes.q: How does the course after a viral illness usually differ in a young child compared with an adult woman?
nodes.a: In children it is acute and usually resolves on its own within weeks to months; in adults it tends to become chronic
nodes.note: Childhood immune thrombocytopenia follows a viral infection or vaccination and often needs no treatment. Adult disease is chronic, more common in women, and may be secondary (HIV, hepatitis C, lupus, chronic lymphocytic leukemia).

nodes.q: Which antibodies cause the low platelet count?
nodes.a: IgG antibodies against platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (sometimes Ib/IX)
nodes.note: A type II hypersensitivity reaction. The count falls because platelets are destroyed in the periphery, not because the marrow fails.

nodes.q: Where are the antibody-coated platelets removed?
nodes.note: Splenic macrophages bind the Fc part of the IgG; this is why splenectomy can help.

nodes.q: What would a bone marrow smear show?
nodes.a: Normal or increased numbers of megakaryocytes
nodes.note: The marrow makes more platelet precursors to compensate; this points to peripheral destruction. Marrow examination is usually not needed.

nodes.q: Which pattern of skin bleeding points to a platelet problem rather than a clotting-factor problem?
nodes.note: Low platelets cause bleeding from small vessels (skin, gums, nose, heavy periods). Clotting-factor defects instead cause deep bleeds into joints and muscles. Low platelets do not cause clots.

nodes.q: Which bleed is the most feared complication when the count is very low?
nodes.note: Risk rises when the platelet count falls below about 10,000/mm3.

nodes.q: What does the blood smear show that separates this from a microangiopathy?
nodes.a: A few slightly large young platelets and no schistocytes (fragmented red cells)
nodes.note: Large platelets show a marrow making new ones. Schistocytes would point to thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura or hemolytic uremic syndrome.

nodes.q: Which retroviral infection must be tested for in every adult with this picture?
nodes.note: HIV is a classic cause of secondary immune thrombocytopenia; hepatitis C is also screened for. An HIV-infected adult with a platelet count of 15,000/mm3 and a normal PT and PTT shows **petechiae and mucosal bleeding** on examination. A low platelet count does not cause deep vein thrombosis.

nodes.q: Which drug is first-line when she has bleeding or a count below about 30,000/mm3?
nodes.note: Glucocorticoids reduce antibody production and slow splenic clearance of coated platelets. Platelet transfusion is kept for life-threatening bleeding because transfused platelets are destroyed too.

nodes.q: Which treatment raises the count fastest when bleeding is severe or surgery is near?
nodes.note: Anti-D immune globulin works in a similar way in Rh-positive patients who still have a spleen.

nodes.q: How does intravenous immunoglobulin slow platelet destruction?
nodes.a: It saturates the Fc receptors on splenic macrophages, so antibody-coated platelets are not engulfed
nodes.note: The effect is fast but lasts only weeks.

nodes.q: Which operation is used when the disease persists after drug treatment?
nodes.note: Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (romiplostim, eltrombopag) and rituximab are alternatives. Give pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccines before the spleen is removed.

nodes.q: Her bruising and low platelets could suggest thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Schistocytes + hemolytic anemia + fever, confusion and kidney injury**; ADAMTS13 deficiency
**Platelets alone are low**; normal hemoglobin and creatinine, alert, no fragmented red cells

nodes.note: The trap: both have purpura and a very low platelet count with a normal PT and PTT.

nodes.q: Her low platelets could suggest hemolytic uremic syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bloody diarrhea (Shiga toxin E. coli) + hemolytic anemia with schistocytes + acute kidney injury**, usually in a child
**Normal hemoglobin, normal creatinine and urea, no schistocytes**

nodes.q: Her bleeding could suggest disseminated intravascular coagulation. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Prolonged PT and PTT + low fibrinogen + high D-dimer**, in a patient made sick by sepsis, trauma or obstetric catastrophe
**Normal PT and PTT** in a well patient

nodes.q: Her mucosal bleeding could suggest von Willebrand disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal platelet count + normal or prolonged PTT + lifelong mucosal bleeding with a family history**
**Low platelet count + normal PTT + new bleeding, no family history**

nodes.q: Her large platelets could suggest Bernard-Soulier syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lifelong bleeding from childhood + giant platelets + absent glycoprotein Ib**, which fails to respond to ristocetin
**Acute onset after a viral illness in someone who never bled before**; only mildly enlarged platelets

nodes.q: Her bruising could suggest aspirin toxicity. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal platelet count + prolonged bleeding time + aspirin use**; irreversible cyclooxygenase block
**Platelet count of 9,000/mm3 and no drug exposure**

nodes.q: Her low platelets could suggest hypersplenism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Enlarged spleen + mild fall in several blood cell lines**, usually from portal hypertension
**Spleen not enlarged + only platelets low and severely so**

nodes.q: Her low platelets could suggest aplastic anemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pancytopenia (low hemoglobin, white cells and platelets) + fatty, empty marrow**
**Normal hemoglobin and white cells**; marrow rich in megakaryocytes

nodes.q: Her gum bleeding and bruising could suggest scurvy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums and a diet with no fruit or vegetables**; normal platelet count
**Low platelet count, good diet, pinpoint spots not centred on hair follicles**

root.stem: A 63-year-old man with known chronic lymphocytic leukemia has had 3 weeks of sudden fatigue and shortness of breath. He is pale with yellow sclerae. His hemoglobin is 6.8 g/dL, leukocyte count 48,000/mm3 and platelet count 180,000/mm3. His reticulocyte count is 9%. Total bilirubin is 4 mg/dL with a direct fraction of 0.5 mg/dL, and urine urobilinogen is increased. The blood smear shows many small round red cells without central pallor and no fragmented cells. He has no family history of anemia or gallstones, has no recent bleeding, and his spleen is not palpable.
root.oneliner: 63M + known chronic lymphocytic leukemia + 3 weeks of sudden fatigue and dyspnea + pallor, scleral icterus + hemoglobin 6.8, reticulocytes 9% + indirect hyperbilirubinemia, urine urobilinogen up + normal platelets + small round red cells without central pallor, no fragments + no family history, no bleeding, no palpable spleen
highlight: small round red cells without central pallor
no family history of anemia or gallstones

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Antibodies coat the red cells and the spleen destroys them. The clincher: **anemia with a high reticulocyte count, raised indirect bilirubin and spherocytes on the smear in a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukemia**; a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test confirms it.

nodes.q: What does his reticulocyte count of 9% tell you about the cause of the anemia?
nodes.a: The marrow is responding; red cells are being lost or destroyed, not underproduced
nodes.note: With raised indirect bilirubin and urobilinogen and no bleeding, this means hemolysis. Lactate dehydrogenase rises and haptoglobin falls. Anemia from underproduction would show a low reticulocyte count.

nodes.q: Why does only the indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin rise?
nodes.a: Heme from the destroyed cells becomes unconjugated bilirubin faster than the liver can conjugate it
nodes.note: It is bound to albumin and is not filtered, so the urine has no bilirubin, but urine urobilinogen is increased.

nodes.q: Which kind of gallstone does long-standing hemolysis produce?
nodes.note: Chronic hemolysis raises bile bilirubin.

nodes.q: Which antibody class coats the red cells in the warm type?
nodes.note: Warm means the antibody binds best at body temperature (37 degrees C). The reaction is a type II hypersensitivity.

nodes.q: Where are the coated cells removed?
nodes.a: By macrophages in the spleen (extravascular hemolysis)
nodes.note: The Fc receptors of splenic macrophages bind the IgG on the cells.

nodes.q: How do splenic macrophages turn his red cells into small round cells without central pallor?
nodes.a: They bite off pieces of antibody-coated membrane (partial phagocytosis), making spherocytes
nodes.note: The cell loses surface area but keeps its volume.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Anti-human globulin added to the patient's washed red cells makes them clump when they are coated with IgG or complement.

nodes.q: Which underlying disease is the likely trigger in this patient?
nodes.note: Lymphoproliferative diseases (chronic lymphocytic leukemia, lymphoma) and systemic lupus erythematosus are the classic causes of the warm type; drugs (penicillin, cephalosporins, methyldopa) are others, and many cases are idiopathic.

nodes.q: Which syndrome is autoimmune hemolytic anemia together with immune thrombocytopenia?
nodes.note: His platelets are normal, so he does not have it.

nodes.q: Which drug is the first-line treatment?
nodes.note: Add folate because active red cell production uses it up. Rituximab or splenectomy for refractory disease, and treat the underlying leukemia. Transfuse only for life-threatening anemia.

nodes.q: His round red cells could suggest hereditary spherocytosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lifelong, family history, gallstones; negative direct Coombs test**; ankyrin or spectrin defect, high mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, positive osmotic fragility or eosin-5-maleimide test
**Acquired, no family history; positive direct Coombs test**; IgG on the red cells

nodes.note: The trap: both have spherocytes, reticulocytosis and indirect hyperbilirubinemia.

nodes.q: His autoimmune hemolysis could instead be the cold type. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **IgM antibody that binds at low temperature and fixes complement; red cell clumps (agglutination) on the smear, painful blue fingers and ears in the cold**; after Mycoplasma pneumoniae or infectious mononucleosis, or with lymphoma; Coombs test positive for complement (C3) only
**IgG antibody at body temperature, spherocytes, no cold symptoms**; Coombs test positive for IgG

nodes.note: Both are autoimmune hemolysis with a positive direct Coombs test; the antibody class decides the type.

nodes.q: His anemia and jaundice could suggest a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia such as thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Schistocytes + low platelets**, often with fever, confusion or kidney injury; negative direct Coombs test
**Spherocytes + normal platelets + positive direct Coombs test**

nodes.q: His hemolysis could suggest hemolytic uremic syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bloody diarrhea + schistocytes + low platelets + acute kidney injury**
**Spherocytes + normal platelets + no kidney injury**

nodes.q: His anemia could be from hypersplenism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Big spleen with mild fall in all three cell lines**; usually portal hypertension
**Spleen not palpable, platelets normal, spherocytes with positive Coombs test**

nodes.q: His anemia and fatigue could suggest acute hemorrhage. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Visible blood loss or a bleeding source; normal bilirubin**; reticulocytes rise only after days
**No blood loss + indirect hyperbilirubinemia + urine urobilinogen increased**

nodes.q: His leukemia could be crowding out the marrow and causing the anemia. How do you tell the two apart?

split.note: **Low reticulocytes with low platelets and low neutrophils**; underproduction, no spherocytes
**Reticulocytes 9% + normal platelets + spherocytes**; the marrow is working

nodes.q: His anemia and chronic illness could suggest anemia of chronic disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low reticulocyte count + low serum iron, low transferrin, high ferritin**; normal bilirubin
**High reticulocyte count + indirect hyperbilirubinemia**

nodes.q: His anemia could be from ineffective erythropoiesis such as vitamin B12 deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low reticulocyte count + macrocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils**; cells die inside the marrow
**High reticulocyte count + spherocytes**; cells die in the spleen

nodes.q: His anemia could suggest a hemoglobinopathy such as thalassemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lifelong, family history, target cells or microcytosis, abnormal hemoglobin electrophoresis**; negative Coombs test
**Sudden onset in adulthood, spherocytes, positive Coombs test**

root.stem: A 5-year-old boy from rural Kenya has had a rapidly enlarging, painless swelling of the right jaw for 2 weeks, with a puffy face and pressure behind both eyes. A single 10-cm firm mass with irregular edges involves the mandible and loosens teeth. There is no fever, no abdominal mass, and no hip or knee pain. A biopsy shows sheets of medium-sized round lymphocytes with many mitoses, scattered pale macrophages that contain nuclear debris, no keratin, no bone or cartilage formation and no rosettes. The cells carry B-cell markers.
root.oneliner: 5M + rapidly enlarging painless jaw mass + puffy face, pressure behind the eyes + from rural Kenya + no fever, no abdominal mass, no bone pain + biopsy: sheets of medium round lymphocytes, many mitoses, pale macrophages with debris, no keratin, bone, cartilage or rosettes, B-cell markers
highlight: rapidly enlarging, painless swelling of the right jaw
no fever, no abdominal mass, and no hip or knee pain
sheets of medium-sized round lymphocytes with many mitoses
pale macrophages that contain nuclear debris
no bone or cartilage formation and no rosettes

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A very fast-growing B-cell lymphoma. The clincher: **jaw mass in a child from an endemic region + 'starry-sky' histology (sheets of lymphocytes with pale macrophages)**.

nodes.q: Which clinical form does this boy have?
nodes.note: Seen in equatorial Africa and parts of Brazil, jaw or facial bones. The sporadic form (United States) usually involves the abdomen, often the ileocecal region, and the immunodeficiency-associated form occurs in HIV infection.

nodes.q: What creates the 'starry-sky' pattern?
nodes.a: Pale benign macrophages with ingested cell debris (tingible body macrophages) scattered among sheets of dark tumor cells
nodes.note: The tumor cells are the dark 'night sky'; the macrophages are the 'stars'.

nodes.q: Which cell death process produces the debris inside the macrophages?
nodes.note: The tumor cells divide so quickly that many die by apoptosis and are cleared by macrophages. The Ki-67 proliferation index is nearly 100%.

nodes.q: Which cell type is the tumor made of?
nodes.a: Mature B lymphocytes from the germinal center
nodes.note: They carry CD (cluster of differentiation) markers CD19, CD20 and CD10.

nodes.q: Which chromosomal translocation drives the tumor?
nodes.a: t(8;14), which moves the c-myc gene next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene
nodes.note: Variant forms use t(2;8) or t(8;22).

nodes.q: What kind of gene is c-myc?
nodes.a: A proto-oncogene encoding a transcription factor that drives cell proliferation
nodes.note: Constant high c-myc expression pushes the cells through the cell cycle.

nodes.q: Which virus is found in nearly all endemic cases?
nodes.note: Co-infection with malaria weakens immune control of infected B cells.

nodes.q: Which metabolic complication can follow when treatment kills the tumor quickly?
nodes.note: Dying cells release potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids: high potassium, high phosphate, high uric acid and low calcium, with acute kidney injury.

nodes.q: Which enzyme drug prevents it by breaking down uric acid?
nodes.note: It converts uric acid to the water-soluble allantoin. Allopurinol, a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, only prevents new uric acid; both are given with vigorous hydration.

nodes.q: Which site needs prophylactic treatment because the tumor spreads there?
nodes.note: Meningeal spread is common in this aggressive lymphoma.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Short, intensive combination chemotherapy (for example cyclophosphamide-based) with rituximab
nodes.note: Most children are cured. Rituximab is an anti-CD20 antibody.

nodes.q: His rapidly growing mass could suggest diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Usually older adults; **large cells, no starry sky**; t(14;18) with BCL2 overexpression in some
Child or young adult; **medium cells, starry sky, t(8;14) with c-myc**; the fastest-doubling human tumor

nodes.note: The trap: both are aggressive B-cell lymphomas that present as a rapidly growing mass.

nodes.q: His jaw lesion could suggest Ewing sarcoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bone pain, fever, onion-skin periosteal reaction on x-ray, small round blue cells that are CD99 positive**; t(11;22) with the EWS-FLI1 fusion gene
**B-cell markers with starry sky and no rosettes**; t(8;14)

nodes.q: His jaw mass could suggest osteosarcoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Malignant cells that make osteoid (bone)**; sunburst pattern and Codman triangle, usually at the knee in adolescents
**No bone or cartilage formation; lymphocytes with B-cell markers**

nodes.q: His facial mass and eye pressure could suggest rhabdomyosarcoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small blue cells that stain for desmin and myogenin; strap-shaped cells with cross-striations**; head and neck or genitourinary sites
**Medium round lymphocytes with B-cell markers and starry sky**

nodes.q: His rapidly growing child tumor could suggest neuroblastoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Abdominal or adrenal mass, high urine homovanillic and vanillylmandelic acid, Homer Wright rosettes, N-myc amplification**
**Jaw mass, no rosettes, c-myc translocation**

nodes.q: His rapidly growing lymphoid mass could suggest Hodgkin lymphoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Reed-Sternberg cells (owl-eye) in a mixed inflammatory background**; painless neck nodes with B symptoms
**Monotonous medium cells and starry sky**; extranodal jaw mass

nodes.q: His head and neck mass could suggest squamous cell carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges**; epithelial cells, older smokers
**No keratin; lymphocytes with B-cell markers**; young child

root.stem: A 9-month-old Black boy is brought in crying with 1 day of painful, swollen hands and feet. He has no fever and no injury. He is pale and mildly jaundiced and has a palpable spleen tip. Hemoglobin is 7 g/dL, reticulocyte count 12%, leukocyte count 9,000/mm3, and indirect bilirubin is increased. The smear shows sickle-shaped cells and target cells. Newborn screening showed hemoglobin F and S but no hemoglobin A. His parents are both healthy.
root.oneliner: 9M + painful swollen hands and feet for 1 day + afebrile, no injury + pallor, mild jaundice, spleen tip palpable + hemoglobin 7, reticulocytes 12%, high indirect bilirubin, normal white count + sickle and target cells + newborn screen: hemoglobin F and S, no A + healthy parents
highlight: mildly jaundiced and has a palpable spleen tip
hemoglobin F and S but no hemoglobin A

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Autosomal recessive; the clincher: **sickled cells on the smear with chronic hemolysis and painful swelling of the hands and feet (dactylitis) in an infant**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.a: Sickle cell anemia (homozygous hemoglobin S disease)
nodes.note: Used for the SS genotype; sickle cell trait (one S gene) is usually symptom-free.

nodes.q: Which amino-acid change creates hemoglobin S?
nodes.a: Glutamic acid replaced by valine at position 6 of the beta-globin chain
nodes.note: A single point (missense) mutation on chromosome 11 (GAG to GTG). The hydrophobic valine lets deoxygenated hemoglobin molecules stick together.

nodes.q: What happens to hemoglobin S when the cell loses oxygen?
nodes.a: It polymerizes spontaneously into long fibers that distort the cell into a sickle
nodes.note: The cell becomes rigid and sticky and blocks small vessels. Hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration and cold trigger it. It is not a failure of the chains to form tetramers and has nothing to do with spectrin.

nodes.q: Why did his symptoms start only after about 6 months of age?
nodes.a: Fetal hemoglobin falls, and fetal hemoglobin prevents polymerization
nodes.note: Fetal hemoglobin (alpha2 gamma2) has no beta chains, so it carries no valine and dilutes hemoglobin S inside the cell.

nodes.q: What causes his swollen, painful hands and feet?
nodes.a: Vaso-occlusion of small bone vessels causing bone marrow infarcts (dactylitis)
nodes.note: Often the first sign of the disease in infants. Older children and adults have painful crises in the long bones, chest and back.

nodes.q: Which process explains his jaundice and reticulocytosis?
nodes.a: Hemolysis of rigid sickled cells, mostly extravascular by macrophages (red cell survival about 20 days)
nodes.note: Some hemolysis is intravascular too. Indirect bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and reticulocytes rise; haptoglobin falls.

nodes.q: Which kind of gallstone forms years later from chronic hemolysis?
nodes.note: They cause biliary colic: postprandial right upper quadrant pain with stones on ultrasound; the elevated bilirubin is unconjugated.

nodes.q: What happens to his spleen over the next few years of repeated infarcts?
nodes.a: It scars and shrinks into a nonfunctioning remnant (autosplenectomy, functional asplenia)
nodes.note: This leaves him open to infection with encapsulated bacteria. Howell-Jolly bodies appear on the smear.

nodes.q: Which encapsulated organism is the leading cause of fatal sepsis in young children with this spleen problem?
nodes.note: Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis and Salmonella are the other encapsulated threats.

nodes.q: While the spleen is still big, which crisis can drop his hemoglobin suddenly and kill him?
nodes.note: Sickled cells pool in the spleen: rapid fall in hemoglobin, rising reticulocytes, a large painful spleen and shock. Seen in infants and young children before autosplenectomy.

nodes.q: Which prophylaxis starts at about 2 months of age?
nodes.note: With pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccines.

nodes.q: Which screening test finds children at risk of stroke?
nodes.note: High cerebral blood flow velocity means high stroke risk; treat with chronic transfusion.

nodes.q: Which lung complication is the leading cause of death in adults with the disease?
nodes.note: Vaso-occlusion in the lung (often with infection or fat embolism): chest pain, fever, hypoxia and a new infiltrate. Treated with oxygen, antibiotics, pain control and transfusion.

nodes.q: Which infection causes a sudden fall in reticulocytes and hemoglobin?
nodes.note: The virus infects red cell precursors, and the marrow stops making red cells.

nodes.q: Which organism is characteristically linked to bone infection in sickle cell disease, far more than in other children?
nodes.note: Infarcted bone and loss of splenic function let Salmonella seed the bone. Staphylococcus aureus remains common, but Salmonella is the classic association.

nodes.q: Which kidney lesion causes hematuria in sickle cell disease and sickle cell trait?
nodes.note: The hypoxic, hypertonic renal medulla promotes sickling and infarcts the papillae. Loss of urine concentrating ability (isosthenuria) is also seen; sickle cell trait is linked to renal medullary carcinoma.

nodes.q: Carrying one sickle gene (sickle cell trait) protects against which infection?
nodes.note: This survival advantage explains why the gene is common in people of sub-Saharan African descent. His healthy parents are each carriers.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis and shows the genotype?
nodes.note: Hemoglobin S predominant, increased hemoglobin F, no hemoglobin A; newborn screening finds it early.

nodes.q: Which drug taken daily reduces the number of pain crises and episodes of acute chest syndrome?
nodes.note: Folic acid, hydration and pain control during crises; transfusion for stroke or acute chest syndrome.

nodes.q: How does hydroxyurea reduce sickling?
nodes.note: It inhibits ribonucleotide reductase; the rise in fetal hemoglobin dilutes hemoglobin S and slows polymerization.

nodes.q: His swollen, painful foot could suggest osteomyelitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, a single warm tender bone, high white count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, positive blood culture** (Staphylococcus aureus; Salmonella in sickle cell disease)
**Afebrile, both hands and feet, hemolytic anemia with sickle cells**

nodes.note: The trap: both give a painful swollen limb in a child with sickle cell disease.

nodes.q: His target cells could suggest hemoglobin C disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Mild hemolysis, many target cells, hemoglobin C crystals; no sickle cells and no crises**
**Sickled cells, painful crises, severe hemolysis; hemoglobin S on electrophoresis**

nodes.q: His severe infant anemia could suggest beta-thalassemia major. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Severe microcytic anemia, little or no hemoglobin A, high hemoglobin F and A2; hepatosplenomegaly and transfusion dependence, no sickling**
**Normocytic anemia with sickle cells and dactylitis; hemoglobin S on electrophoresis**

root.stem: A 68-year-old man has had 6 months of headaches, blurred vision, and an intense itch after hot showers. His face and hands are ruddy and he has a palpable spleen 5 cm below the left costal margin. He has never smoked, has no lung disease or sleep apnea, and lives at sea level. Oxygen saturation on room air is 98%. Hemoglobin is 21 g/dL, hematocrit 61%, leukocyte count 15,000/mm3 with 4% basophils, and platelet count 500,000/mm3. The smear shows occasional giant platelets, leukocyte alkaline phosphatase is increased, serum erythropoietin is low, and a test for the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene is negative.
root.oneliner: 68M + 6 months of headache and blurred vision + itch after hot showers + ruddy face, spleen 5 cm below costal margin + never smoked, no lung disease or sleep apnea, sea level + oxygen saturation 98% + hemoglobin 21, hematocrit 61%, WBC 15,000 with basophils, platelets 500,000 + giant platelets, high LAP, low erythropoietin + BCR-ABL1 negative
highlight: no lung disease or sleep apnea, and lives at sea level
Oxygen saturation on room air is 98%

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A myeloproliferative neoplasm in which the marrow makes too many red cells (and often white cells and platelets) on its own. The clincher: **high hemoglobin with normal oxygen saturation, low erythropoietin and splenomegaly, with itching after a hot shower**.

nodes.q: Which gene mutation drives the disease in nearly all patients?
nodes.a: JAK2 V617F (a gain-of-function mutation in the Janus kinase 2 gene)
nodes.note: JAK2 sits downstream of the erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor receptors, so the signal stays on without the hormone. Test for it to confirm.

nodes.q: At which level of the marrow does the primary defect arise?
nodes.a: The hematopoietic stem cell (multipotent myeloid stem cell)
nodes.note: Because the mutation is in the stem cell, red cells, granulocytes and platelets all rise, not only red cells. A defect limited to the erythroid progenitor would raise red cells alone.

nodes.q: Why is serum erythropoietin low?
nodes.a: Negative feedback: the high red cell mass suppresses the kidney's production
nodes.note: Erythropoietin is high in secondary polycythemia.

nodes.q: What causes the itch after a hot shower?
nodes.a: Release of histamine and other mediators from increased basophils and mast cells
nodes.note: Basophils are high on his count. Burning pain in the fingers and toes (erythromelalgia) is also seen.

nodes.q: Which neutrophil enzyme level is raised, in contrast to chronic myeloid leukemia?
nodes.note: It is low in chronic myeloid leukemia.

nodes.q: Which complication causes most of the deaths?
nodes.note: Thick blood and abnormal platelets: stroke, myocardial infarction, deep vein thrombosis, and portal or hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari syndrome). Bleeding from abnormal platelets also occurs.

nodes.q: Which metabolic complication follows the high cell turnover?
nodes.note: Uric acid is a breakdown product of purines from nucleic acids.

nodes.q: What is the first treatment?
nodes.a: Phlebotomy to keep the hematocrit below 45%, plus low-dose aspirin
nodes.note: Aspirin lowers the thrombosis risk.

nodes.q: Which drug is added for high-risk patients (age over 60 or previous thrombosis)?
nodes.note: It inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and so blocks DNA synthesis. Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, is used when hydroxyurea fails.

nodes.q: Which late changes can follow after years?
nodes.a: Spent-phase myelofibrosis (marrow scarring) and transformation to acute myeloid leukemia
nodes.note: The spleen grows further as blood is made outside the marrow.

nodes.q: His high hematocrit could suggest secondary polycythemia from chronic hypoxia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low oxygen saturation (COPD, high altitude, sleep apnea) or an erythropoietin-secreting tumor; high erythropoietin**; no splenomegaly, normal white cells and platelets
**Normal oxygen saturation + low erythropoietin + splenomegaly + high white cells and platelets**

nodes.note: The trap: both have a high hemoglobin and hematocrit.

nodes.q: His high white count and big spleen could suggest chronic myeloid leukemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Very high white count with all stages of granulocytes, low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL1)**; hemoglobin not raised
**Raised hemoglobin and hematocrit, high leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, JAK2 mutation, BCR-ABL1 negative**

nodes.q: His high platelet count could suggest essential thrombocythemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Isolated platelet count above 450,000/mm3** (often over 1 million); hemoglobin normal; JAK2, CALR or MPL mutation
**Hemoglobin and hematocrit also high + low erythropoietin**

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An overactive, enlarged spleen that traps and destroys blood cells. The clincher: **splenomegaly + mild low counts in more than one cell line + a working marrow (high reticulocytes), with normal coagulation tests**.

nodes.q: Why is the spleen enlarged in this patient?
nodes.a: Raised pressure in the portal and splenic veins causes congestive splenomegaly
nodes.note: Cirrhosis scars the liver and blocks portal flow.

nodes.q: How does the big spleen lower the blood counts?
nodes.a: Cells are pooled in the enlarged red pulp and removed by splenic macrophages (sequestration)
nodes.note: Up to about 90% of platelets can be trapped in a big spleen, compared with about a third normally.

nodes.q: What does the reticulocyte count tell you about his marrow?
nodes.a: The marrow is working and compensating (cellular or hyperplastic marrow)
nodes.note: It shows that the cytopenias come from peripheral destruction, not marrow failure.

nodes.q: Which result after treatment would confirm that the spleen was the cause?
nodes.a: The blood counts return toward normal after splenectomy or splenic embolization
nodes.note: Together with splenomegaly, cytopenia and a cellular marrow, this completes the classic criteria.

nodes.q: Why are his clotting studies normal despite the bruising?
nodes.a: The bruising comes from low platelets, not from a clotting factor problem
nodes.note: Mild thrombocytopenia from splenic pooling; liver failure can add a prolonged prothrombin time, but here the clotting tests are normal.

nodes.q: Which life-threatening bleed shares the same high pressure?
nodes.note: Portal hypertension opens portosystemic collaterals at the lower esophagus.

nodes.q: What is the main management?
nodes.a: Treat the portal hypertension (non-selective beta-blocker, variceal screening and banding); splenectomy or partial splenic embolization only for severe symptoms
nodes.note: Splenectomy risks portal vein thrombosis. Vaccinate against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b first.

nodes.q: Which drug class lowers portal pressure?
nodes.note: Beta-1 blockade lowers cardiac output and beta-2 blockade leaves unopposed splanchnic vasoconstriction by alpha receptors, so portal inflow falls.

**Normal coagulation tests and fibrinogen + big spleen**; counts mildly low

nodes.note: The trap: both give petechiae with low platelets in a patient with liver disease.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A rare, indolent B-cell leukemia of middle-aged men. The clincher: **pancytopenia + big spleen without lymph node enlargement + lymphocytes with hair-like projections that are tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) positive**.

nodes.q: Which gene mutation is found in nearly all cases?
nodes.note: BRAF is a serine/threonine kinase of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK: RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK) growth signaling pathway; the mutation keeps it permanently switched on.

nodes.q: Which tests confirm the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Flow cytometry showing CD11c, CD25 and CD103 on B cells
nodes.note: Also test for the BRAF V600E mutation. TRAP staining is the classic older stain.

nodes.q: Why did the bone marrow aspiration fail?
nodes.a: Marrow fibrosis (reticulin) and packing with hairy cells give a dry tap
nodes.note: A bone marrow biopsy is needed instead, and shows hairy cells with a 'fried egg' look.

nodes.q: Which part of the spleen do the leukemic cells fill?
nodes.note: Most lymphomas spread to the white pulp; red pulp infiltration gives massive splenomegaly and adds sequestration to the pancytopenia.

nodes.q: Which blood cell type is characteristically missing?
nodes.note: His monocyte count is 1%. The loss invites atypical mycobacterial and other opportunistic infections; infection is the main cause of death.

nodes.q: What is the first-line treatment?
nodes.note: A single course gives long remissions in most patients; pentostatin is an alternative. Rituximab or a BRAF inhibitor for relapse.

nodes.q: How does cladribine kill the cells?
nodes.a: It is a purine analogue resistant to adenosine deaminase that builds up in lymphocytes and triggers apoptosis
nodes.note: Pentostatin instead inhibits adenosine deaminase, which is toxic to lymphocytes.

nodes.q: His lymphocytes and big spleen could suggest chronic lymphocytic leukemia. How do you tell them apart?

**Pancytopenia with hair-like projections, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase positive, no lymph nodes, dry tap**

nodes.note: The trap: both are B-cell leukemias in older patients with splenomegaly and lymphocytes on the smear.

**Hairy lymphocytes, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase positive, BRAF V600E**
